## wine (207)

### Acidity

`·` **Grapes contain both tartaric and malic acid. Why does tartaric matter more to the winemaker?**
  It is the stronger and far more stable of the two, and it largely survives fermentation and ageing. Malic is respired away by the vine in warm conditions and can be converted by MLF. Tartaric is what ultimately underpins the finished wine's pH.

`Q` **Two dry whites both hold 7 grams of acid a litre, yet one is far more fragile. What is pH measuring that the total is not?**
  Titratable acidity is how much acid is there, found by neutralising it. pH counts the hydrogen ions that acid actually released, on a backwards scale where low means sharp, and it is what sets microbial risk and colour. Sourness tracks the total; stability tracks pH.

### Albariño

`·` **In Rías Baixas on Spain's wet Atlantic coast, Albariño is trained on pergolas overhead. Why?**
  Rain, well over 1300mm of it a year. A canopy lifted head high on stone pergolas lets wind through to dry the bunches and keeps them off the damp ground, because rot is the region's central problem. Albariño's unusually thick skins are part of the same answer.

### Alsace

`·` **Alsace is one of France's most northerly wine regions. So why are its whites so ripe?**
  The Vosges mountains take the rain out of the westerly weather, leaving Colmar among the driest towns in France. Sun and dry autumns push ripeness far, so an Alsace wine can be dry or distinctly sweet and taste ripe either way. Since 2021 an Alsace white must say which.

`Q` **Alsace names 51 grand cru vineyards. What does the title stop a grower doing on that land?**
  Reserved for Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat, with named exceptions: Sylvaner at Zotzenberg, blends at Kaefferkopf and Altenberg de Bergheim, and red Pinot Noir on three sites since 2022. Classified rows carrying Pinot Blanc are bottled as plain Alsace.

### Alto Adige

`Q` **Alto Adige is Italy's most northerly wine region, deep in the Alps, and most of its output is white. Why whites there?**
  Altitude and aspect in an Alpine valley. Vineyards climb past 1000m on steep sides, so nights are cold and the season long, which is what aromatic whites want. Pinot Grigio and Gewurztraminer are taken seriously here in a way they are not further south.

### Argentina

`·` **Argentina plants vines above 1000m and as high as 3000m. What does altitude buy besides cool nights?**
  Ultraviolet light. The berry defends itself by loading its skin with anthocyanin, the colour pigment, and with tannin, so high-altitude Malbec comes out darker and firmer than the same grape grown low. The air is dry too, so almost every vine is irrigated from Andean snowmelt.

### Australia

`Q` **Coonawarra is a narrow strip of red soil over limestone in a flat, cool corner of South Australia. Why Cabernet?**
  Terra rossa: a thin band of red clay loam over limestone, barely a dozen kilometres long. It drains freely and the site is cool for Australia, so Cabernet holds acidity and a leafy, minty lift over its blackcurrant. Warmer, lower Barossa Shiraz goes the other way.

`Q` **Hunter Valley Semillon is picked early, sees no oak and goes into bottle at about 11%. Why does it then age for decades?**
  Picked before the sugar builds, it holds very high acid and almost no primary fruit, so a young one tastes thin and neutral. Nothing is laid over it and nothing is waiting to drop out. A decade in bottle builds toast, honey and lanolin out of the wine itself.

`Q` **Margaret River sits on a peninsula with ocean on three sides of it. What does that buy its Cabernet?**
  Maritime moderation. Water warms and cools slowly, so the swing between day and night, and between one month and the next, is unusually small and the fruit ripens gradually. Cabernet finishes there without the baked, jammy edge a hot inland site gives it.

`Q` **Tasmania is too cool to ripen most of what Australia is known for. What has it become instead?**
  Base wine for sparkling. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir grown that cool arrive high in acid and low in sugar, which is wrong for a still wine and right for a second fermentation. The island also makes still Pinot that reads far closer to Burgundy than the mainland does.

`Q` **McLaren Vale's oldest Grenache stands as unirrigated bushes on deep sand. Why is that fruit now sought after?**
  Dry-grown old bush vines on deep sand carry very little fruit and root a long way down for water, so the berries come in small and concentrated. Grenache was planted here for fortified wine and nearly pulled out when that market died. What survived makes the region's best reds.

### Austria

`·` **In the vineyards of Austria's Wachau, Riesling takes the stone terraces and Grüner Veltliner the ground below. Why?**
  Water. The terraces are bare primary rock, gneiss and granite, holding almost none, and Riesling handles that stress and takes its edge from it. Grüner Veltliner, Austria's own white grape, is thirstier, so it sits on the loess below: wind-blown silt that holds moisture.

`Q` **One Wachau bottle says Federspiel and the next says Smaragd. What is that ladder measuring?**
  Ripeness at harvest, expressed as finished alcohol, because every tier is dry. Steinfeder stops at 11.5%, Federspiel runs 11.5–12.5%, Smaragd starts at 12.5%. The word on the label promises weight and says nothing about sweetness.

`Q` **Zweigelt was made at an Austrian research station in 1922 by crossing two local grapes. What was the breeder after?**
  A crossing is two varieties of one species bred on purpose. St. Laurent buds early and meets spring frost; Blaufränkisch, the dark peppery Austrian red, ripens so late autumn rain catches it. Zweigelt buds after one and ripens before the other, and is Austria's most planted red.

`Q` **Blaufränkisch buds early and ripens late, which is the worst pair of habits a vine can have. Where does Austria grow it?**
  Burgenland, on the Pannonian plain around the Neusiedlersee, where hot dry summers run into long warm autumns: the season this grape needs to finish at all. It is Lemberger in Germany and Kékfrankos in Hungary, and it pours dark and firm with high acid and a peppery edge.

### Barossa

`Q` **The Barossa and Eden Valleys are neighbours in South Australia. Why is one known for Shiraz and the other for Riesling?**
  Height, not distance. Barossa vineyards sit around 250m and Eden Valley ones between roughly 380 and 550m, enough to slow ripening by one to three weeks. That late, cool finish holds the acidity Riesling needs, while the warm valley floor builds the Shiraz.

### Beaujolais

`Q` **A bottle says Fleurie and the word Beaujolais appears nowhere on the label. What is it?**
  The top of three tiers: Beaujolais, Beaujolais Villages, then ten crus in the granite hills of the north, which carry only their own names. Granite gives firmer wine than the clay and sandstone of the flat south, so Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent can age where simple Beaujolais cannot.

### Bordeaux

`Q` **Why is the Left Bank of Bordeaux planted to Cabernet Sauvignon and the Right Bank to Merlot?**
  Soil, not latitude. The Left Bank's deep gravel drains hard and stores heat, which late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon needs to finish. Right Bank clay and limestone hold water and stay cooler, and Merlot buds and ripens early enough to cope with that.

`Q` **Burgundy's crus rank vineyards. What does the 1855 classification rank?**
  Properties, not plots. Brokers ranked the estates of the Médoc by what their wines sold for, and the rank has belonged to the name ever since. A classed growth that buys neighbouring land can bottle that fruit at its rank. A grand cru boundary cannot move.

`Q` **Saint-Émilion reclassifies its châteaux roughly every ten years. What follows from a rank that can be lost?**
  The rank has to be re-earned on a dossier of tastings, terroir and reputation, so it can go down as well as up. Cheval Blanc, Ausone and Angélus withdrew across 2021 and 2022 rather than be judged, leaving Pavie and the newly promoted Figeac alone at the top.

`Q` **One Bordeaux label says Saint-Émilion Grand Cru and the next says Grand Cru Classé. What separates them?**
  Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is an appellation, not a prize. Any grower on the same ground may use it by cropping lower, reaching a higher minimum alcohol and ageing longer. Grand Cru Classé is the ranked list inside it, and most bottles saying Grand Cru are not on it.

`Q` **A Bordeaux château sells its grand vin, the wine under the château's own name, and a second wine beside it. What decides which lots go where?**
  Selection. Young vines, parcels that underperformed and the hard wine pressed from the drained skins are all held out, so the grand vin can be chosen more tightly. That is why second wines spread as standards rose, and why one can drink well, and early.

`Q` **The Médoc has a saying that the best vines see the river. What is the Gironde actually doing for them?**
  A large body of water warms and cools slowly, so it holds off spring frost and takes the edge off a heat spike. The gravel is the same story: the river laid those banks down, so the deepest and best-draining of them lie nearest it. The saying tracks two things at once.

`Q` **Pessac-Leognan is the only corner of Bordeaux ranked for its whites as well as its reds. Why there?**
  Mixed ground in one place. The same deep gravel that finishes Cabernet runs beside patches of sand and clay where Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon do well, so estates make both seriously. The 1959 Graves list ranks them for each colour separately.

`Q` **Pomerol holds some of the most expensive wine on earth and has no classification at all. How does a buyer navigate it?**
  Reputation, unranked. It is tiny, there is no list and no tasting panel, so the market simply prices what it trusts. Soil does much of it: a seam of dense clay under part of the plateau holds water for Merlot in a dry year, and the estates sitting on it are the famous ones.

### Burgundy

`·` **Two growers bottle Chambertin Grand Cru. Why can the wines differ so much?**
  Because Burgundy classifies land, not producers. Le Chambertin is one vineyard divided among many owners, each with their own parcels, viticulture and winemaking. The classification guarantees the site; it says nothing about the execution.

`·` **Chablis has seven grand crus and they sit side by side on one hill. Why all in one place?**
  Aspect, at the northern limit of ripe Chardonnay. That slope above the river Serein faces south west and takes the most sun in the region. It sits on Kimmeridgian marl, a clay and limestone packed with fossil oyster shells. Petit Chablis is mostly on younger rock above.

`Q` **A list offers Gevrey-Chambertin, and Chambertin at ten times the price. Same place?**
  In 1847 the village of Gevrey annexed the name of its greatest vineyard, and others down the Côte d'Or followed, as far as the two Montrachets. A grand cru is its own appellation and stands alone on the label, so the bare vineyard name outranks the hyphenated village every time.

`Q` **A Burgundy label reads Meursault, with a second name under it in smaller type. What is that second name?**
  A lieu-dit is simply what a parcel is called on the map. A village wine may print it, but the law holds those letters to half the height of the appellation name so it cannot pass for a cru. Plenty are excellent sites. The name promises the place and nothing above it.

`Q` **Burgundy's ladder runs regional, village, premier cru, grand cru. What may a grower do with fruit off a grand cru row?**
  The ladder only runs downward. Each step up covers less ground and caps the yield harder. A grower may always declassify into a name beneath his own, and never into one above it. That is why a village wine from a great address can drink so far above its label.

`Q` **A Burgundy label prints the word Monopole beneath the vineyard name. What does that change?**
  Nearly every Burgundian cru is split between dozens of owners, so there is always a rival bottling off the same ground to judge a grower by. A monopole has one owner and one reading of the site, and nothing beside it to argue with. La Tâche and La Romanée are two.

`Q` **Burgundy's grand crus sit in a band partway up the slope, never at the top and never at the bottom. What is wrong with each end?**
  Mid-slope is the compromise. Above it the soil thins toward bare rock and the wind and cold bite. Below it the washed-down soil is deep and fertile, holds water, and cold air pools there on a spring night. The band between drains freely, warms early and keeps just enough soil.

`Q` **The Cote de Nuits is almost entirely red and the great white grand crus all sit in the Cote de Beaune. What splits them?**
  Geology, followed by habit. Marl heavy in clay and limestone runs through the southern half in bands that suit Chardonnay, while the Nuits sits on ground where Pinot Noir has long done better. Nothing forbids either grape; four centuries of growers simply settled it.

`Q` **The Maconnais makes Chardonnay at a fraction of Cote de Beaune prices, from the same grape. What is different?**
  Latitude and lie. Southern Burgundy is warmer and its slopes gentler, so Chardonnay ripens more easily and gives a broader, softer, earlier-drinking wine. Pouilly-Fuisse holds the best sites, and it finally got premier crus of its own in 2020.

### Cabernet Franc

`·` **Why does Bordeaux keep Cabernet Franc in the blend when Cabernet Sauvignon makes the bigger wine?**
  Insurance and perfume. It buds and ripens a week or so earlier, so it finishes on cool, damp clay where Cabernet Sauvignon would stay green. It also brings lighter tannin and a violet lift. And it is the parent of both Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.

### Cabernet Sauvignon

`Q` **Cabernet Sauvignon is the most planted grape on earth. What makes it travel so well?**
  It holds its shape. Thick skins and small berries give colour, tannin and acid almost anywhere. The aroma runs a legible line too: green pepper when underripe, then blackcurrant, then cassis and cedar when ripe. Growers get a wine buyers recognise.

### Cahors

`Q` **Cahors in south west France is Malbec's original home. How does its wine differ from an Argentine Malbec?**
  Cahors is cooler and much damper, so tannin ripens slowly and the wine finishes firm and savoury rather than plush. Medieval buyers called it the black wine. The appellation must be at least 70% Malbec, with only Merlot and Tannat beside it.

### Campania

`Q` **Taurasi in Campania is called the Barolo of the south. What does its Aglianico share with Nebbiolo?**
  The structure and the calendar. Aglianico holds high acidity over dense tannin and hangs into late October or November on volcanic slopes around Taurasi and Mount Vulture, so it needs years in bottle. It is far darker than Nebbiolo, which is the tell.

### Central Coast

`Q` **Santa Barbara grows cool-climate Pinot Noir further south than Los Angeles. How is that possible?**
  The mountains lie the wrong way, and it is a gift. Almost the whole American coast runs north to south, but the transverse ranges here run east to west, opening the Santa Ynez and Santa Maria valleys straight to the Pacific. Cold air and fog pour in, and it gets warmer inland.

### Champagne

`Q` **One Champagne says Blanc de Blancs and the next Blanc de Noirs, and both pour pale gold. What differs?**
  Which of the three grapes went in. Blanc de Blancs is Chardonnay alone, taut and citrus-driven, and it ages long. Blanc de Noirs is Pinot Noir and Meunier pressed gently enough that no colour comes off the skins: broader and redder-fruited. Most Champagne blends all three.

### Chardonnay

`·` **Chardonnay is called neutral. Why is that a reason to plant it rather than a complaint?**
  It carries little aroma of its own, so what reaches the glass is site and cellar rather than grape: the same variety reads lean and stony in Chablis, at Burgundy's cold northern tip, and broad and buttery from a warm site fermented in barrel. It also ripens early almost anywhere.

### Chile

`·` **Chile re-cut its wine map east to west in 2011. What do Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes describe?**
  How much cooling a site gets, rather than how far south it sits. Costa sits in reach of the cold Humboldt current off the Pacific. Andes takes night air draining off the mountains. Entre Cordilleras, between the ranges, is the warm central floor. A valley name hid all of it.

`Q` **Chile spent over a century growing what it believed was Merlot. What did DNA testing find in 1994?**
  Carmenere, a Bordeaux variety phylloxera had all but wiped out in France. It ripens a good two weeks after Merlot, so picking the mixed rows on Merlot's schedule left it green and pyrazine-heavy. Given its own harvest date it comes in dark, savoury and soft.

### Châteauneuf

`Q` **Two red Châteauneuf-du-Pape wines, from the southern Rhône, taste nothing alike. How much does the appellation fix?**
  It permits thirteen varieties by name, or eighteen if the white, grey and black versions of some of them are counted apart, and then sets no percentages. White grapes may go into the red. So one bottle is nearly pure Grenache and its neighbour a field blend.

`Q` **In Châteauneuf-du-Pape, in the southern Rhône, the best-known vineyards are carpeted in big round stones. What do those galets do?**
  Two things at once: they take up heat through the day and give it back overnight, and they cap the soil so less water evaporates out of it. Not every fine parcel has them, which is the catch. Some of the best sites are deep sand, and those give the perfumed, lighter wines.

### Climate

`·` **Why does vintage matter far more in Chablis than in the Languedoc, at opposite ends of France?**
  Chablis sits at the northern margin of viable Chardonnay, where spring frost and poor flowering weather regularly threaten both crop size and ripeness. Warm, dry regions ripen reliably every year, so the differences between vintages are much smaller.

`Q` **Where does the green pepper note in an underripe Cabernet come from?**
  A compound the grape already holds. Methoxypyrazines smell of capsicum at vanishingly low concentrations, and they fall as the fruit ripens and the bunch sees sun. Cool sites, big crops and shaded canopies keep them, which is why growers strip leaves from the fruit zone.

`·` **A cool-climate grower adds sugar before fermentation and a warm-climate one adds acid. What is each fixing?**
  Chaptalisation adds sugar to the juice so the yeast makes more alcohol. It does not sweeten the wine, because that sugar ferments away. Acidification adds tartaric acid to fruit that ripened too fast to keep its own. EU rules allow one or the other, never both.

### Closures

`Q` **Cork or screwcap. What is a bottle closure actually deciding?**
  Oxygen ingress, which is a dial and not a seal. A tin-lined screwcap admits almost nothing, keeping a wine fresh but leaving it liable to smell of struck match. Natural cork admits more, varies bottle to bottle, and carries the risk of cork taint.

### Douro

`Q` **The Douro's terraces were planted for Port, so where do its dry red wines come from?**
  Fruit that cannot legally become Port. Each year the trade body fixes how much of the harvest may be fortified, then shares that benefício out by a vineyard grade running A to F. Anything beyond a grower's share ferments dry instead. The same terraces make both.

### Faults

`Q` **A corked wine smells of damp cardboard. What else has the taint done to it?**
  TCA does not only add a musty smell, it suppresses olfactory signalling, so it takes aroma away as well. A lightly tainted bottle reads as dull and fruitless rather than obviously faulty, which is the version most people pour and blame on the wine.

`Q` **One of these faults can genuinely improve in the glass. Which?**
  Reduction: volatile sulfur compounds left by the yeast, which air can drive off, so a decant or a hard swirl often clears it. The other three are one-way. TCA, the trichloroanisole taint behind a corked bottle, oxidation and volatile acidity do not come back.

`Q` **A red smells of farmyard and sticking plaster, and the same case gets louder year on year. What is at work?**
  Brettanomyces needs only traces of sugar and hides in the pores of old oak. It turns acids the wine already holds into compounds that smell of horse, leather and plaster, and being alive it carries on in bottle. Low acidity and light sulphur let it in.

`Q` **A wine smells clean in the glass, then leaves a stale, cereal, mouse-cage aftertaste. What happened?**
  The compounds behind it stay locked in a non-volatile form at wine's low pH and only become smellable once saliva raises the pH in your mouth. There is nothing to find in the glass. Dab a drop on the back of your hand and smell there. Roughly a third of people cannot perceive it.

`Q` **One wine smells of vinegar and another of nail polish remover. Is that the same fault twice?**
  Linked but separate. Acetobacter needs oxygen and turns ethanol into acetic acid, which reads as vinegar somewhere around 600 to 900mg a litre. That acid then esterifies with ethanol into ethyl acetate, which reads as nail polish at about 12mg. You usually meet the ester first.

`Q` **Wildfire smoke crossed a vineyard and the young wine tasted clean. Why can that change after bottling?**
  The vine defends itself by locking smoke phenols onto sugars, in which form they have no smell. Fermentation and then slow acid hydrolysis in bottle cut them loose, so an ashy, medicinal note can arrive months later. Filtering strips the free phenols but not the bound ones.

### Food

`·` **Why does a good red fall apart next to asparagus or a soft-boiled egg?**
  Umami raises the perception of bitterness, astringency and acidity, so a tannic wine turns hard and hollow against it. Salt is the counterweight and does the opposite, softening tannin and acid, which is why seasoning the dish often rescues the pairing.

`Q` **A fine dry Riesling turns thin and sour beside a fruit tart. What has the sugar in the dish done to it?**
  Sweetness on the plate raises the acidity and bitterness you read in the glass, and strips out the wine's own sweetness and fruit. So a dry wine goes hollow and sharp. The working rule: the wine has to be at least as sweet as the dish, or it loses.

`Q` **A squeeze of lemon goes over the fish, and the wine that worked a minute ago tastes flat. What has the acid on the plate done?**
  Acid in the dish lowers the acidity you register in the glass, and pushes the wine's fruit and body forward. So a soft wine goes flabby and a sharp one is rescued. The working rule: the wine needs at least as much acid as the food.

`Q` **A hot curry beside a ripe red at 15%. Why does the burn get worse rather than better?**
  Alcohol lands on the same receptor. Capsaicin, the compound behind chilli heat, is read by one that also answers to ethanol, so alcohol stacks onto the burn instead of washing it away. Sugar and cold damp it down, which is why an off-dry Riesling at 9% copes.

`Q` **Why does a hard, tannic red read softer against a fatty cut of beef than it does on its own?**
  Astringency is not a taste but a drag: tannin disrupts the slippery film that keeps the surfaces of the mouth sliding, and you feel the friction. Fat lays that film back down. So the richness has to be real, and a lean fillet does far less than a fatty rib.

`Q` **The local wine with the local dish is the oldest advice in wine. What is that rule actually worth?**
  It is a tested habit rather than a mechanism, and nothing about shared soil is doing the work. So it fails wherever either side has moved since. Tomatoes reached Italy after Columbus, and Chianti today is a different wine from the one the habit grew around.

### Fortified

`·` **Why is Fino fortified to about 15% and Oloroso to about 17%?**
  Flor yeast survives only to roughly 15.5% abv. Below that the flor layer lives and shields the wine from oxygen: biological ageing, which gives Fino its saline, bready character. Above it the flor dies and the wine ages oxidatively, giving Oloroso its nutty, dried-fruit profile.

`Q` **Madeira, the fortified wine from a Portuguese island out in the Atlantic, is deliberately heated in production. What does that heating buy?**
  The wine is cooked on purpose, oxidised and caramelised before it is ever sold. Because that damage has already been done deliberately, air and time can do very little more to it: an open bottle keeps for months where a table wine keeps days. The heating is estufagem.

`Q` **Almost no sherry carries a vintage. What is the system behind that?**
  The solera. Casks sit in rows by age: a portion is drawn from the oldest row, the solera itself, which is refilled from the next youngest, a criadera, and so on up. Nothing is ever emptied, so young wine is folded into old for ever and age becomes an average.

`Q` **A bottle says Cream Sherry, from Jerez in southern Spain. What is in the glass?**
  A dry base, usually Oloroso, blended with sweet wine once it has aged. Pedro Ximénez grapes are laid out in the sun until they are half raisin, so the must is too sugary to ferment far. Sweetness in sherry is nearly always added at the end.

`Q` **A dry Fino sherry sold en rama, meaning raw, pours hazy and smells far louder than the standard bottling. What was left out?**
  The filtering. Sherry is normally filtered hard to stay bright on a shelf, which strips the solids carrying its texture and the smell of flor, the yeast film it ages under. En rama is drawn in spring when the flor is thickest, and bottled almost untouched. Drink it soon.

`·` **Banyuls and Maury, sweet reds from Roussillon on France's border with Spain, are fortified while still on their skins. What does that buy?**
  Grape spirit goes into the must while it is still fermenting. Left on the skins, it keeps macerating in alcohol for days after the yeast dies, and alcohol pulls out colour and tannin that water cannot reach. The addition is mutage, the category vin doux naturel.

### Germany

`·` **A bottle says Spätlese. Is the wine sweet?**
  Not necessarily. Prädikat levels measure must weight, the sugar in the grapes at harvest, not residual sugar in the finished wine. A Spätlese can be fermented bone dry and labelled Spätlese Trocken.

`Q` **Mosel Riesling grows on steep slopes of dark slate. What is the slate mainly doing?**
  Buying ripeness at the edge of where it is possible. At fifty degrees north the sun is low, so a steep slope meets it closer to square, and broken dark slate absorbs that heat and releases it overnight. The slatey note in the glass is a tasting term, not dissolved rock.

`·` **Germany's Prädikat ladder ranks ripeness. So how does a great vineyard get named?**
  Separately, and by the growers first. The VDP, a private association, built a four-tier pyramid of origin topped by Grosse Lage, whose dry wine is bottled as Grosses Gewächs. The 2021 wine law copied that shape into statute, binding from 2026, though regions are still ranking sites.

`Q` **Two German Rieslings, one labelled Trocken and one Feinherb. What separates those two words?**
  Trocken is bound by law: broadly 4 grams of sugar a litre, stretching to 9 where acidity nearly matches the sugar. That is why a dry Riesling can taste rounder than the word suggests. Halbtrocken runs to about 12. Feinherb means nothing legally and sits loosely off-dry.

`Q` **A Mosel label reads Piesporter Michelsberg and another reads Piesporter Goldtröpfchen. Are both single vineyards?**
  Germany writes a single vineyard, an Einzellage, as village plus site. A Grosslage, one name covering a large group of vineyards, is written in exactly the same shape. Michelsberg is one of those, so the form of the name cannot tell you which you are holding.

`Q` **A German white comes in a squat flattened flask instead of a tall bottle. What does that shape tell you?**
  The Bocksbeutel belongs to Franken and its use is protected in EU law. Franken is Germany's most continental region, hard winters and an early autumn, so its grape is Silvaner rather than late-ripening Riesling, and the wine is nearly always dry and savoury.

`Q` **A German shelf carries Spätburgunder, Weissburgunder and Grauburgunder side by side. What are those three?**
  Pinot Noir, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris, which are one variety and two colour mutations of it. Burgunder names the family and spät means late, for the red's ripening. Germany is now the world's third-largest grower of Pinot Noir, mostly in Baden and the Ahr.

`Q` **German ripeness levels climb from Kabinett up to Trockenbeerenauslese. What is the picker doing differently at the top?**
  The ladder measures sugar in the grape, and above Spätlese it is bought by sorting. Auslese means selected bunches, Beerenauslese selected berries, Trockenbeerenauslese shrivelled ones taken singly. Eiswein sits outside it: whole frozen berries, pressed while the water is ice.

### Gewurztraminer

`Q` **Gewurztraminer smells of rose and lychee and ripens to high sugar. Why does a warm site ruin it?**
  It has no acid to spare. It ripens early to a lot of sugar and sheds acid on the way, so a warm site gives a broad, soft wine at 14% with nothing holding it up. Cool sites keep some bite under the perfume. Its pink skins are why it pours deep gold.

### Greece

`Q` **On Santorini the vines are woven flat into low coiled baskets on the ground. What is that shape for?**
  Wind and water. The island is scoured by the meltemi, its summer wind, and gets almost no rain. So the vine is trained into a coiled basket, a kouloura. The fruit sits inside it, sheltered from wind and sun, and the basket gathers dew off the night mist.

`Q` **Naoussa's Xinomavro pours pale, browns young and grips hard. Which far better known grape does that describe?**
  Nebbiolo, and the resemblance is close enough that tasters mistake the two blind. The name means acid black: high acidity over dense tannin with very little pigment, and a tomato and dried-herb character. It wants years, and Naoussa in Macedonia is its home.

`Q` **Santorini's vines are among the oldest in Europe and not one of them is grafted. Why has phylloxera never taken hold?**
  The ground. Phylloxera cannot move through pure sand, so the island never needed American rootstock. Vines grow on their own roots. They are renewed by bending a cane back into the soil to root, so one plant can be centuries old while its wood stays young.

### Grenache

`·` **Grenache ripens to very high sugar but makes pale, soft wine. Why is it so often blended?**
  It brings alcohol, red fruit and a sweet texture, and not much else: low in pigment and tannin, and quick to oxidise. Syrah supplies colour and firmness, Mourvèdre tannin and savoury weight. The Southern Rhône blend is a structure the grape cannot build alone.

`Q` **Spain's old Garnacha vineyards are nearly all on high, poor, awkward ground. Why is that where the old vines are left?**
  Fashion and subsidy. Garnacha was written off as bulk wine and pulled out through the 1990s for Tempranillo and French varieties, and what got replanted was the flat, irrigable ground. What nobody bothered to pull sits high and poor, which is where the grape is good.

### Italy

`Q` **A shelf holds Montepulciano d'Abruzzo beside Vino Nobile di Montepulciano. Are these related?**
  A pure coincidence of names. Montepulciano is a grape, grown mostly in Abruzzo on the Adriatic side, giving deep, soft, low-acid red. Vino Nobile comes from the hill town of Montepulciano in Tuscany and is made from Sangiovese. Nothing connects them but the word.

### Jerez

`Q` **Palomino, the sherry grape, makes a flat and neutral table wine. Why is that an advantage in Jerez?**
  Everything you taste in sherry arrives after fermentation, from flor, the film of yeast a Fino ages under, or from air. A grape with a voice would be in the way. Palomino is low in acid and nearly scentless, and grows almost only on albariza, a white chalk that holds winter rain.

### Jura

`Q` **A bottle from the Jura, in eastern France, holds 62cl where a standard bottle holds 75cl. What is that size recording?**
  Vin jaune sits in barrel six years and three months and is never topped up, under a voile: a film of yeast that shields it from the air. About 38% evaporates away, and that short bottle, the clavelin, holds what a litre became. The grape is Savagnin.

### Labelling

`·` **A label says old vine. What does that guarantee?**
  Almost nothing. The term is unregulated in most of the world. The underlying mechanism is real: lower vigour, smaller yields, and deep roots that buffer drought. But with no legal minimum age it stays a claim rather than a specification.

`Q` **One Burgundy says mis en bouteille au domaine and the next carries only a merchant's name in Beaune. What separates them?**
  Who owned the grapes. Bottled at the domaine means the estate grew the fruit and bottled it itself. A négociant buys grapes, juice or finished wine and sells under its own name, so one appellation can be assembled from many growers. A cooperative is a shared cellar its members supply.

`Q` **One Italian label says Classico and the next says Superiore. What is each word promising?**
  Classico is geography: the historic core of a zone, kept as a name when the boundary was widened around it. Superiore is a specification, usually a higher minimum alcohol and a lower yield, sometimes a little ageing. One says where, the other says how ripe the fruit came in.

### Languedoc

`Q` **Why does a bottle of Pays d'Oc name its grape when a Minervois grown up the road does not?**
  Different tiers, different promises. An appellation such as Minervois fixes which varieties may be planted and in what proportion, and offers the place name as the guarantee, so the grape stays off the label. Pays d'Oc is an IGP, a looser tier, and it allows the grape.

`Q` **Carignan was pulled up across southern France as bulk-wine material and is now sought out there as old vines. What changed about it?**
  Carignan will carry an enormous crop and ripens very late, so the south planted it by the hectare and the wine came out hard, sharp and hollow. Old bush vines on poor schist crop a fraction of that and do ripen, and the grape then pours dark and savoury.

### Loire

`·` **How does one Loire grape make bone dry, sweet and sparkling wine equally well?**
  Chenin Blanc holds very high acidity even when fully ripe, so sugar never reads as flabby and the base wine is taut enough for sparkling untouched. Thin skins take botrytis readily, and bunches ripen unevenly, which is why the sweet wines are picked in several passes.

`Q` **A bottle of Vouvray, a Loire Chenin Blanc, says nothing at all about sweetness. What could be inside?**
  One appellation covers the whole scale: sec for dry, demi-sec for off-dry, moelleux for sweet. Printing the word is voluntary for still Vouvray and plenty of growers leave it off. Low alcohol is the usual hint that fermentation was stopped with sugar still in.

`·` **A Muscadet label says sur lie. What does that phrase bind the producer to?**
  The wine stays on its fermentation lees through the winter, then goes into bottle straight off them, never racked. That keeps the dissolved carbon dioxide you feel as a faint prickle. Sur lie is simply on the lees. Muscadet is the place, Melon de Bourgogne the grape.

`Q` **A wine list offers a red Sancerre. What grape is in it, and why is it not the one Sancerre is famous for?**
  Sancerre is one appellation in three colours, and its red and rosé must be Pinot Noir. It lies nearer Burgundy than the Atlantic and was largely red until phylloxera, the root-eating aphid, wiped the vineyard out and Sauvignon Blanc went back in its place.

`Q` **Sancerre's growers name three different soils and price the wines by which one. What do those soils actually change?**
  Drainage. Marl holds water and gives the broadest, slowest-maturing wine; limestone gravel drains hard and gives the most aromatic; flint drains hardest and gives the tautest, with the smoky note growers call gunflint. Pouilly-Fume sits across the river on the same seam.

`Q` **One Chinon is light and crunchy, the next firm enough to cellar. Both are Cabernet Franc. What separates them?**
  Where on the valley it grew. Gravel terraces by the Vienne warm fast and give the light, floral, chill-it style. The tuffeau limestone slopes above hold water and ripen slower, giving structure and the graphite edge that lets a Chinon run twenty years.

### Merlot

`Q` **Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot ripen in one vineyard. What makes the Merlot softer?**
  Colour and tannin sit in the skin and the juice sits in the pulp, so the ratio between them decides extraction before a winemaker touches anything. Cabernet's small thick-skinned berries give far more skin per litre. It is also why rain before harvest thins a wine.

### Mourvèdre

`·` **Mourvèdre is a minority partner across most of southern France but leads in Bandol. What limits it?**
  It ripens very late and needs real heat to finish. Picked short it comes out hard and green with a gamey edge that never resolves, so growers plant much of it only where autumn stays warm. Bandol, on the Mediterranean coast, requires at least half of it.

### Napa

`Q` **Napa Cabernet routinely finishes above 15% alcohol and Bordeaux rarely does. Why?**
  Sugar ripeness and phenolic ripeness, meaning the softening of tannin and the loss of green aromas, run on different clocks. In heat the sugar arrives first, so a grower who holds on for the tannin picks fruit already carrying 15% of potential alcohol. Hang time is bought with alcohol.

### New York

`Q` **The Finger Lakes grow Riesling at a latitude where winter can kill a vine outright. What makes it survivable?**
  The water. The lakes are deep enough not to freeze, so they give back stored warmth through the winter and hold the air above the shore above the killing point. They also delay budbreak in spring, which keeps the vine out of the frost. Slopes furthest from water are the riskiest.

### Oak

`·` **Why would a winemaker choose fourth-fill barrels that impart almost no flavour?**
  For texture rather than flavour. The extractable oak compounds are largely spent, but the barrel still allows slow oxygen ingress, which polymerises tannin and stabilises colour. Neutral oak is a deliberate tool, not a compromise.

`Q` **Traditional Rioja smells of coconut and sweet dill. Where does that come from?**
  The species of tree. American white oak carries much more cis oak lactone than French oak, and that single compound smells of coconut. Rioja bought American casks for generations, so a note that belongs to a forest reads as the signature of a region.

`Q` **Two Chardonnays spend a year in the same new oak barrels and one tastes far more of oak. What did the other do differently?**
  Barrel fermentation puts the ferment inside the wood. Yeast turns vanillin, the compound behind the vanilla note, into a far quieter one, and the lees take up wood tannin as they settle. Ferment in steel first and the oak lands on top of the wine, not into it.

### Oregon

`Q` **Oregon's Willamette Valley is the New World region most often set beside Burgundy. What makes the comparison fair?**
  Not the rock but the weather. The valley lies open to the Pacific through a gap in the Coast Range, so it is cool, cloudy and wet. Vintage genuinely matters there, and rot is a live threat. That marginality, rather than the soil, is what it shares with Burgundy.

### Piedmont

`Q` **Barolo is pale and browns young. Why is it also one of the most tannic wines made?**
  Colour and grip are different compounds, and a grape can be short of one and loaded with the other. Nebbiolo has little anthocyanin and what it has is unstable, so it goes orange at the rim early. Depth of colour tells you nothing about structure.

`Q` **Barolo and Barbaresco are the same grape grown a few miles apart. Why does Barbaresco drink well younger?**
  Both are Nebbiolo and neither may hold anything else. Barbaresco lies lower, nearer the Tanaro river and warmer, so its tannin ripens earlier. The rules follow the fruit: Barolo needs 38 months of ageing with 18 in wood, Barbaresco 26 with 9.

`Q` **Barolo from La Morra drinks earlier than Barolo from Serralunga d'Alba. What is behind that?**
  The zone straddles two geological eras. The western communes, La Morra and Barolo among them, sit on younger bluish marl heavy in clay, which gives perfume and a softer frame. Serralunga and Monforte sit on older, sandier, iron-tinged rock that gives firmer tannin and a longer wait.

`Q` **A Barolo label prints Cannubi or Bussia under the appellation. Is that a cru in the Burgundian sense?**
  Barolo mapped and named 170 vineyards in 2010, plus its eleven communes. The boundary is official and the yield is cut a little, but the list is deliberately flat: nothing in the rules says one site beats another. The hierarchy is real and it lives in the market, not in law.

`Q` **Barbera and Dolcetto grow side by side in Piedmont and are easy to confuse. Which is which in the glass?**
  They are opposites. Barbera pours dark and juicy, high in acid over soft tannin, so it drinks young. Dolcetto is the reverse: low acid with firm, faintly bitter tannin, and its name, little sweet one, points at that soft acidity. It ripens weeks earlier than Nebbiolo too.

### Pinot Noir

`Q` **Pinot Noir is called a difficult grape. What actually makes it difficult in the vineyard?**
  Early budding puts it in the path of spring frost, and thin-skinned berries packed tightly together trap moisture and rot in a wet autumn. Those same thin skins give little pigment and little tannin, which is why the wine is pale and why nothing hides a mistake.

`Q` **Marlborough and Central Otago both make New Zealand Pinot Noir. Why do the two taste so unalike?**
  Climate shape and ground. Central Otago is the country's only continental region, inland, hot by day and cold by night on free-draining schist: dense, dark-fruited, structured. Marlborough is maritime on alluvial gravel, and gives lighter, herbal, red-fruited Pinot.

### Port

`·` **Port is not back-sweetened. So why is it sweet?**
  The ferment is stopped early. Neutral grape spirit goes in at around 6–8% abv and kills the yeast while a large amount of grape sugar is still unfermented. The sweetness is leftover must, not an addition.

`·` **Ruby and tawny Port begin as the same wine. What actually separates them?**
  Air. Tawny matures in seasoned casks small enough to let oxygen in, which fades the colour to amber and builds nut, fig and caramel. Ruby is held in large vats or tank with almost no air, keeping its purple and its fruit. Age follows from the vessel, not the reverse.

`·` **Why is Port fruit trodden or pumped so hard, and so early?**
  The window is short. Fortifying at roughly half the sugar ends fermentation after about two days, and skin contact ends with it. All the colour and tannin the wine will ever have comes out inside that time. That is what a lagar is: a shallow granite trough to tread in.

`Q` **A Vintage Port and a Late Bottled Vintage from the same harvest stand side by side. What separates them?**
  Time in wood, and what that leaves to do afterwards. Vintage goes into bottle at about two years and matures there for decades, unfiltered, so it throws a crust and must be decanted. LBV is usually filtered on bottling, pours clear and is ready on release.

### Portugal

`Q` **A bottle of Vinho Verde is not green. So what is the verde describing?**
  Verde means young rather than green. This is the far north of Portugal, and the wine goes out within months of picking, often at only 9 to 11% alcohol. The faint prickle began as an accident, a bacterial fermentation finishing in the bottle, and is now usually gas added at bottling.

`Q` **Touriga Nacional is Portugal's most prized red grape, and growers still plant very little of it. Why?**
  Yield. Left alone it sets a tiny crop of small, thick-skinned berries. That is exactly why the wine is so dark and perfumed, and exactly why a grower paid by weight avoids it. It anchors Port blends and, on the granite of the Dao, makes floral, firm dry reds.

`Q` **In the Alentejo some wine is still fermented and kept in tall clay jars sunk into the floor. What does the clay do?**
  Slow air and no wood. Unlined clay lets a trace of oxygen through the wall much as a cask does, so the wine softens. But it contributes no vanilla, no toast and no tannin of its own. Vinho de Talha became a protected category in 2010, reviving a Roman practice.

### Priorat

`Q` **In Priorat, inland from Barcelona, old Garnacha and Carinena vines climb steep slopes of crumbling black slate. What does that ground do?**
  Llicorella, a friable slate that roots can split. Water sits deep and nowhere else, so vines drive down for it and carry very little fruit. The wine comes out concentrated, high in alcohol and firm, which is why Priorat sits at a price its neighbours do not.

### Producers

`Q` **A cooperative buys its members' grapes by weight. What does that do to the wine it makes?**
  A member is paid for what the trailer weighs, and cutting his crop to improve it costs him money. That is the structural reason so much cooperative wine is clean, cheap and anonymous. The ones that climbed out of it now grade fruit parcel by parcel and pay different rates for it.

### Provence

`Q` **Provence, on France's Mediterranean coast, makes rose as its main product rather than a by-product. What does that change in the vineyard?**
  The decision moves back to the vine. Where rose is the plan, growers pick earlier, for acidity and pale colour, not the phenolic ripeness a red needs. Sites and varieties are chosen for it too. A rose bled off a red ferment comes from fruit picked for something else.

### Rhône

`·` **What actually separates the Northern from the Southern Rhône?**
  Grape and terrain. In the north Syrah is the only black grape permitted, worked on steep granite terraces in a continental climate. The south is Mediterranean, flatter and many times larger, and its reds are Grenache-led blends where no one variety carries the wine.

`·` **Southern Rhône vines are often grown as low free-standing bushes with no wires. Why?**
  The mistral, a cold dry wind that funnels down the valley and can gust past 90km/h. A gobelet bush sits low, takes the wind without shredding and shades its own fruit. That same wind dries the canopy after rain, which is why so much of the region farms organically.

`Q` **Côte-Rôtie co-ferments up to a fifth of white Viognier with its Syrah. Tradition says this fixes the colour. Does it?**
  Co-fermentation is the tradition and copigmentation the theory, but trials find no colour benefit and a loss at high proportions. What survives is an aromatic lift, real but more modest than the story around it. Viognier also ripens before Syrah, not after.

`Q` **Hermitage is one granite hill of about 130 hectares. Why is that hill worth more than the flat land beside it?**
  Aspect. The Rhone runs roughly north to south, so its slopes mostly face east or west. At Tain the hill swings round and presents a broad south face to the sun. At this latitude that is what finishes Syrah. Cote-Rotie is the same trick on a smaller scale.

`Q` **Gigondas sits above Cotes du Rhone in the southern ladder, on the same Grenache. What earns the step up?**
  Site and crop. The vineyards climb the limestone teeth of the Dentelles de Montmirail, so nights fall cooler than on the plain and the fruit keeps acidity. The cru caps yields well below the regional appellation, and the wine comes out firmer and longer.

### Riesling

`·` **Where does the petrol note in an older Riesling come from?**
  TDN, a compound that builds in the bottle out of carotenoids, the pigments the grape uses to handle sunlight. Sun exposure, heat and water stress load the fruit with the precursors, which is why Australian Riesling can show petrol young and Mosel often never does.

`Q` **Riesling is among the greatest white grapes and is almost never put in new oak. Why not?**
  There is nothing for oak to do and plenty for it to bury. Riesling's lift comes from light aromatic compounds that vanilla and toast smother, and its acidity is the point rather than a problem to round off. Where wood is used it is old and large, so it breathes without flavouring.

### Rioja

`·` **What does Gran Reserva actually guarantee?**
  Only maturation. For reds: at least 60 months in total, of which a minimum of 24 in oak and 24 in bottle. It says nothing about vineyard site or fruit quality. A producer can bottle an outstanding wine as Genérico if they choose to age it differently.

`Q` **Rioja Alavesa and Rioja Oriental lie at opposite ends of one region. What separates them?**
  Rioja runs about 100km along the Ebro and climbs to the west. Alta and Alavesa sit high at the cool end, sheltered from Atlantic rain by the Sierra de Cantabria, and give the firmer, finer wines. Oriental, lower and hotter, is Mediterranean, and Garnacha ripens there to real weight.

`Q` **Since 2017 a Rioja label may read Viñedo Singular. What does that phrase certify?**
  An origin, not an ageing term. The 2017 rules built a ladder of place beside the old one: zone, then village, then a single plot at the top. That plot must be at least 35 years old, hand-picked, cropped well under the regional limit, and passed by two tastings.

### Rosé

`Q` **One rosé is barely pink and the next is deep salmon. What usually separates them?**
  Skin time, in hours. Press red grapes at once and the juice runs almost colourless; a few hours on the skins darkens it. Colour tells you nothing about sweetness. Blending red into white is barred for still rosé in the EU and allowed for sparkling, which is how pink Champagne is made.

`Q` **A rosé label says the wine was made by saignée. What was it a by-product of?**
  Juice is run off a red ferment in its first hours, so what stays behind holds more skin per litre and finishes darker and firmer. The pink juice drawn away ferments on its own, and is usually weightier than a rosé from fruit picked for pink. Saignée means bleeding.

### Rueda

`Q` **Rueda sits on the high Castilian plateau of northern Spain, where summer days are fierce. How does its Verdejo stay fresh?**
  Height and the dark. Vineyards sit around 700 to 800m, so nights fall hard even in August and the fruit holds acidity. Most of the crop is machine-picked overnight to bring it in cold, because Verdejo oxidises readily. It gives a bitter-almond finish that is its signature.

### Sangiovese

`Q` **Brunello di Montalcino and Chianti Classico are both Sangiovese. Why may Brunello use nothing else?**
  Warmth. Montalcino lies south of Chianti Classico, warmer and drier, and Sangiovese ripens there fully enough to carry a wine by itself: Brunello must be 100% of it. Chianti Classico is cooler, keeps a sharper red-fruited bite, and may fill out with up to 20% of other red grapes.

### Sauvignon Blanc

`Q` **Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc smells of passionfruit far louder than a Loire one. Where is that aroma made?**
  In the ferment. The grape carries thiols, sulphur compounds smelling of passionfruit and grapefruit, but bound to amino acids where they have no smell at all. Yeast enzymes cut them loose, so the strain and the handling decide how much ever arrives.

### Service

`·` **What does serving a tannic red too cold actually do to it?**
  Cold raises the perception of acidity and bitterness, tannin included, and slows the release of aromatic compounds. Warmth does the reverse and pushes alcohol forward. So an over-chilled red reads hard and mute, and a warm one reads sweet and spirity.

`Q` **A young tannic red and a forty-year-old one both get decanted. Same reason?**
  Two different jobs. A young wine is decanted for oxygen, which lifts the aroma and takes the edge off the tannin. An old one is decanted only to leave its sediment behind. The aromas decades built can fade within the hour, so pour gently and drink it soon.

`Q` **A shop sells a different glass for every grape. What does the shape of a glass reliably change?**
  Aroma, in two steps. The bowl sets how much surface the wine can evaporate from, and the taper decides how much of that vapour is funnelled to your nose. So how far you fill it counts as much as its shape: filled to the brim, a glass collects nothing.

`Q` **Reds at room temperature, whites from the fridge. What is wrong with following that as written?**
  Room temperature is a phrase from houses nobody heated, nearer 16C than a modern 21C. So most reds reach the table too warm, and most whites too cold. Traffic in the glass runs one way as well: it warms in the hand and never cools. Err cold.

`Q` **Half a bottle is left over. What actually decides whether it is still worth drinking in three days?**
  Oxidation, and its rate is set by the area of wine meeting air and by temperature. So the two moves that work are cutting the headspace, by pouring what is left into a smaller bottle, and refrigerating it, reds included. Delicate whites and old reds go first.

`Q` **Opening sparkling wine, you hold the cork still and turn the bottle. Why that way round?**
  Five to six atmospheres sit behind that cork, several times a car tyre, and the bottle is doing the work of ejecting it. Gripping the cork and rotating the low-friction base means metering a cork that is already moving rather than fighting one. Keep a thumb over it throughout.

`Q` **Wine goes out white before red, dry before sweet, young before old. What is that order protecting?**
  Tannin binds and strips the proline-rich proteins in saliva, and the mouth takes eight to fifteen minutes to rebuild that film. Sugar masks in much the same way. So a tannic or sweet wine poured early flattens everything after it. Palate management, not etiquette.

### Sicily

`Q` **Etna is one of the southernmost vineyards in Europe, yet its reds come out pale and sharp. What allows that?**
  Height, on a mountain that is still building itself. Vines run from about 400m past 1000m up the flanks, so nights stay cold and the harvest can reach November. Nerello Mascalese, the main red grape, is thin-skinned and pale in the way Nebbiolo is, with acid and tannin but little colour.

### Sonoma

`Q` **Some of Sonoma's coolest vineyards lie south of its warmest. What breaks the usual rule that south means warmer?**
  Where the coast range breaks. Cold Pacific air and fog pour through gaps such as the Petaluma Gap and up the Russian River. So a site's distance from an opening decides its temperature more than its latitude. Two vineyards an hour apart can be different climates.

### South Africa

`Q` **Pinotage was bred at the Cape in 1925 by crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsault. What was the breeder trying to fix?**
  Abraham Perold, the Cape's first professor of viticulture, wanted Pinot Noir's quality on a vine that could take the heat and disease there. Cinsault, known locally as Hermitage, was hardy and reliable. The cross ripens early, and pushes a banana or acetone note when the ferment runs warm.

`Q` **South Africa holds more Chenin Blanc than anywhere on earth, and most of it was planted for brandy. What changed?**
  Nothing in the vineyard. Chenin, called Steen there, went in by the thousand hectares for distilling and bulk, much of it old, dry-grown bush vine on poor ground. Once anyone troubled to crop it low and ferment it in barrel it turned out to make world-class white.

`Q` **The Cape sits at a latitude that ought to be far too hot for fine wine. What holds it in balance?**
  Cold water, and the wind off it. The Benguela current runs up the west coast out of the Southern Ocean, and the south-easter blows off it all summer, the wind locals call the Cape Doctor. How near a vineyard sits to that water shapes its style more than its latitude.

### Sparkling

`·` **Where does the biscuit and brioche character in Champagne come from?**
  Autolysis. The second fermentation happens inside the bottle, and the dead yeast cells then break down in contact with the wine under pressure. Tank-method wines finish their second fermentation in a pressurised tank with little lees contact, so they keep primary fruit and florals instead.

`·` **The second fermentation leaves dead yeast inside the bottle. How does it get out?**
  Riddling, then disgorgement. The bottle is tilted and turned until the sediment gathers in the neck, the neck is frozen, and the cap comes off so the pressure fires the plug clear. The gap is topped up with the dosage, and that sugar sets brut or demi-sec.

`·` **Most Champagne carries no vintage year. What is the blender actually doing?**
  Erasing the harvest. A house holds back reserve wines from earlier years and blends them into the new base, so the non-vintage bottle tastes the same whenever you buy it. That consistency is the house style, and it is the product. A vintage is declared only when one year can stand alone.

`Q` **One grower bottles the same Champagne at zero sugar and at nine grams a litre. What actually changes?**
  Sugar suppresses the perception of acid and lends a little weight, so one wine reads taut and severe and the other rounder. It is why a zero dosage Champagne, bottled with no sugar added at all, needs a ripe and long-aged base: nothing is laid over its edges.

`Q` **Champagne is pressed in fractions and some houses use only the first. What is wrong with the juice that follows?**
  The first 2050 litres from a 4000kg press is the cuvée: clean, sharp and long-lived. The 500 litres of taille squeezed after carry more colour and more potassium, and potassium strips acidity out. Taille gives a fruitier wine young and a tired one at ten years.

`Q` **One Prosecco says Brut and the bottle beside it says Extra Dry. Which is the sweeter wine?**
  The words stopped meaning what they say. The EU ladder runs Brut Nature 0–3 grams a litre, Extra Brut 0–6, Brut 0–12, then Extra Dry 12–17 and Dry 17–32. The plainer the word sounds, the sweeter the wine. Extra Dry is Prosecco's usual style.

`·` **Prosecco takes its second fermentation in a sealed pressurised tank rather than inside each bottle. What does that decide?**
  Cost, and the shape of the fizz. The tank method ferments a whole batch at once in weeks, so nothing is handled bottle by bottle or locked in a cellar for years. Prosecco is also finished nearer 3 atmospheres than Champagne's 5 or 6, so its foam is softer and falls away faster.

`Q` **Champagne labels usually carry two small letters, NM or RM or CM. What are they recording?**
  Who grew the fruit and who made the wine. NM, négociant manipulant, buys grapes, and nearly every famous house is one. RM, récoltant manipulant, is a grower making wine from its own vines. CM is a cooperative selling its members' wine, and MA is a buyer's own brand made by someone unnamed.

`Q` **Cava is Spain's bottle-fermented sparkling wine. Which part of Spain does the name point to?**
  Almost all of it, oddly. Cava was defined by how it is made rather than where, so the name reaches municipalities from Catalonia out to Rioja, Aragón, Valencia and Extremadura, now in four zones. Ageing is the ladder: nine months, eighteen for Reserva, thirty for Gran Reserva.

### Storage

`Q` **One bottle sits five years at a steady 18C, another swings from 10C to 20C every day. Which fares worse?**
  A steady 18C only ages a wine faster than a cold cellar would. A daily swing pumps it up the neck and back, drawing air in and eventually pushing wine past the capsule. Light is the other one: blue wavelengths turn a white or a sparkling wine oniony, which is why the glass is green.

`Q` **A wine cellar is kept damp, at around 70% humidity. Why, when the wine is sealed inside glass?**
  The wine is sealed in glass but the cork is not: its outer end sits in the room. Dry air pulls water out of it and it shrinks away from the neck, which is also why bottles lie down, to keep the inner end wet. A screwcap wants none of this.

`Q` **Most wine is at its best on release. What does the small minority that improves in bottle actually have?**
  Fruit is the part time takes away, so a wine needs something left standing once it has gone: acid, tannin, sugar, or the spirit in a fortified one. Nothing fattens in bottle. A wine that is thin now will only ever be thin and old later.

### Structure

`·` **Someone calls a wine firm. How do you work out whether they mean acid or tannin?**
  Acid is a taste. You register it at the sides of the tongue and it makes you salivate. Tannin is tactile: it binds salivary proteins and leaves the mouth dry. A high-acid, low-tannin Riesling and a low-acid, high-tannin red both feel firm, for opposite reasons.

`Q` **Two young reds from one grape, one at pH 3.4 and one at pH 3.9. What is different in the glass?**
  Anthocyanin, the skin pigment, only shows its red form in strongly acid conditions. The pH scale runs backwards, so 3.9 is the less acid of the two. In it more pigment shifts to colourless and blue forms, and the rim reads dull and brown. Low pH also slows browning.

`Q` **A tasting note says a wine has structure and says nothing at all about fruit. What has that word named?**
  Structure is the frame you feel rather than smell: acid, tannin, alcohol and any sugar. Aroma and fruit are the flesh over it. Balance is those two in proportion, not the components being low, so a bone dry, hard, sharp wine can be perfectly balanced.

`Q` **Why does a tannic red genuinely feel softer after fifteen years?**
  Not by leaving. Thirty and fifty year verticals show aged reds holding tannin concentrations close to young ones, so precipitation is not the main story. The tannin itself rearranges into forms that bind salivary protein weakly, and weak binding is what the mouth reads as soft.

### Sweet wine

`Q` **What does noble rot, a fungus deliberately welcomed onto ripe grapes, add that simply leaving them to shrivel does not?**
  Concentration is the easy half: the fungus pierces the skin, water evaporates out, and sugar and acid both climb. The rest is its own chemistry, which builds notes no raisined grape carries. It wants misty mornings and dry afternoons; left wet, the same fungus ruins the crop as grey rot.

`Q` **Tokaji Aszu, Hungary's great sweet wine, picks the berries noble rot has shrivelled one at a time, then does not ferment them. What happens to them?**
  Aszú berries are mashed to a dough and steeped in must or wine of the same vintage. So the sugar is drawn out rather than fermented in, and a slow, incomplete ferment follows. A puttony was the 25kg hod. Since 2013 every Aszú must reach 120 grams of sugar a litre.

`Q` **Sauternes, upriver of Bordeaux, gets reliable noble rot almost every year while its neighbours do not. What does it have that they lack?**
  A river junction. The cold Ciron runs into the warmer Garonne, and the temperature difference throws up mist most autumn mornings that burns off by afternoon. Damp then dry is exactly the cycle botrytis needs; stay wet and the same fungus becomes grey rot.

### Syrah

`Q` **Northern Rhône Syrah tastes of cracked black pepper and Barossa Shiraz almost never does. What decides that?**
  Rotundone, the compound that smells of black pepper. It builds late in ripening and only where the bunch stays cool and shaded; sun and heat break it down. Syrah and Shiraz are one grape, so what changes across the world is the temperature, not the vine.

### Tasting

`·` **A technically dry wine reads as slightly sweet. What is happening?**
  Ethanol itself tastes faintly sweet at moderate concentration, and glycerol adds body, so high-alcohol dry wines can read off-dry. Where acidity is too low to balance that alcohol, the same wine reads hot instead.

`·` **Tasting notes sort aromas into primary, secondary and tertiary. What is that sorting?**
  Where the smell came from. Primary is the grape and the site: fruit, flower, herb, pepper. Secondary is the making: yeast and bread, butter, vanilla and toast off the oak. Tertiary is time: nut, dried fruit, mushroom, leather. Placing a smell tells you what the wine has been through.

`Q` **A taster holds the wine, swallows, then breathes out through the nose. Why not simply sniff the glass harder?**
  Flavour is mostly smell, and smell has two doors: in at the nostrils, and up the back of the throat from the mouth, the retronasal route. Warmed to body temperature, the wine gives up heavier compounds a cool glass never released. So the finish smells unlike the nose.

`Q` **A taster calls one wine intense and the next one long. What is each of those words measuring?**
  Two separate clocks. Intensity is how loud the wine is while it is in the mouth; length is how many seconds the flavour holds after you swallow, and finish is the character of what stays. A loud oaky red can be short and a quiet Riesling long.

`Q` **Wine runs back down the inside of the glass in slow legs. What does that actually tell you?**
  Ethanol evaporates faster than water, which raises surface tension in the film and drags wine up the wall until it beads and falls back. More alcohol, faster cycle. Glycerol adds a little viscosity and very little else. Legs are a rough alcohol reading, never a quality one.

`Q` **A tasting exam marks you against a fixed word list rather than on whether your meaning was clear. Why?**
  A scale only works if everyone reads it the same way. Fixing the words to a set of scales makes one taster's note comparable with another's and with the key. The cost is that a near-miss word scores nothing, even where a person would have understood you perfectly.

`Q` **Working blind toward a grape, a taster ranks clues by how far they can be trusted. What sits at the top?**
  Three tiers. A compound the plant carries is strongest: methoxypyrazine points at the Cabernet family, rotundone at Syrah, thiols at Sauvignon. Site clues such as acidity come next. Winemaking clues, oak and malolactic, are weakest, because anyone anywhere can choose them.

### Tempranillo

`·` **Tempranillo takes its name from ripening early. What does that cost the grower?**
  Acidity. It reaches sugar and colour fast and drops acid on the way, so on a warm site the wine finishes soft and short. Rioja answers with altitude and cool nights, and with blending partners: Garnacha for body, Graciano and Mazuelo for the acid and lift Tempranillo runs out of.

`Q` **Tempranillo makes a blacker, harder wine in Ribera del Duero than it does in Rioja. What is doing that?**
  Ribera vineyards run from roughly 750m to 1000m on the Castilian plateau, so days are hot, nights near freezing and the season short and frost-bitten. Berries stay small, and the local strain of the grape, Tinto Fino, is smaller-berried again. More skin, less juice, darker wine.

### Terroir

`Q` **A producer says the wine expresses its terroir. What is that word actually claiming?**
  Terroir gathers the whole of a site: soil and subsoil, slope, aspect and its own local climate, and in French usage the practice that grew up to suit them. The claim it makes is narrow and testable, that a site marks its wine across vintages and across owners.

### Trade

`Q` **A ten pound bottle holds far more than twice the wine of a five pound one. What does that arithmetic?**
  Excise is charged on alcohol, not on quality, so the same cash comes off both bottles. Add glass, closure, shipping and everyone's margin, and a cheap bottle has almost nothing left for the liquid. Nearly every extra pound you spend goes into the wine itself.

### Tuscany

`Q` **Why was Tignanello, from the heart of Chianti Classico, sold as Vino da Tavola?**
  Chianti then dictated the varieties and required a share of white grapes. Dropping them and adding Cabernet Sauvignon put the wine outside its own name, so it went out as table wine. A classification binds what you may blend, not only where you may pick.

`Q` **Chianti Classico has three tiers. What does Gran Selezione require that Riserva does not?**
  Estate fruit. Riserva may be made from bought grapes; Gran Selezione may not, and it ages thirty months against twenty four. From the 2027 harvest it also needs 90% Sangiovese and only Tuscan grapes beside it, so no Cabernet and no Merlot.

`Q` **A shelf holds Chianti beside Chianti Classico. What is the relationship between those two names?**
  Chianti Classico is the historic zone between Florence and Siena. In 1932 the Chianti name was stretched over a far larger area around it and the old core kept the word Classico. The two became separate appellations in 1996, and Classico crops lower and holds more Sangiovese.

### Valpolicella

`Q` **Amarone and Recioto della Valpolicella both begin with grapes dried on racks for months. What separates them?**
  Where the ferment is allowed to stop. Corvina and the other grapes of Valpolicella, in the hills above Verona, lose water on the racks into winter, concentrating sugar. Run the ferment out and every gram becomes alcohol: Amarone, dry and near 16%. Halt it and you have Recioto.

`Q` **A Valpolicella label, from the hills above Verona, says Ripasso. What was the wine passed back over?**
  The skins of a finished Amarone. Young Valpolicella is run onto them, and the sugar still in them restarts a short fermentation. The wine gains roughly a degree of alcohol, colour, tannin and a dried-fruit depth. Amarone is the dry wine made from grapes shrivelled on racks.

### Veneto

`Q` **Soave is one of Italy's best-known white appellations and its grape is Garganega. What does Garganega actually bring?**
  A quiet grape that carries its site. Garganega ripens late, holds acidity, and gives almond, white blossom and a saline finish rather than obvious fruit. The best sites are the volcanic hills of Soave Classico; the flat land below is where the name was spent.

### Viognier

`Q` **Viognier is picked riper than almost any other white grape. What forces that?**
  The perfume that makes the grape worth growing builds in the last days on the vine, and a Viognier picked before it smells of very little. Waiting costs acidity and adds alcohol, which is why Condrieu, its home in the northern Rhône, is full, oily and soft.

### Viticulture

`·` **Why does a large diurnal temperature range help red wine quality?**
  Warm days drive photosynthesis and phenolic ripening, and the berry burns off malic acid faster as it warms. Cool nights slow that loss, so the fruit gains sugar and colour while holding acidity. Trials suggest the night alone matters less than the season's warmth.

`Q` **Almost every vine in the world is two plants joined at the base. Why?**
  Phylloxera, an aphid that eats roots. It reached Europe in the 1860s and killed the European vine, whose roots cannot wall off the damage, while American species grew up with it and can. So European fruiting wood is grafted onto American roots. Chile, isolated and sandy, never had to.

`Q` **Why is a low yield not on its own a promise of ripe fruit?**
  Ripening is a supply problem: the leaves make the sugar and the crop spends it. Growers reckon on roughly a square metre of healthy leaf for every kilo of fruit. A cramped, shaded vine carrying a tiny crop can still fall short of ripeness.

`Q` **A grower prunes in the cold of January. Why is that when next autumn's crop size is largely fixed?**
  The buds being counted formed the previous summer, and each already carries the bunches it will push out. Winter pruning decides how many of them stay, so the crop is set before a leaf appears. A dull, shaded summer costs the following harvest as well as its own.

`Q` **Leaves are pulled from around the bunches. Why does the date it is done change what it buys?**
  Pull before flowering and the vine has less sugar to set fruit with. Fewer berries take, so the bunch comes out small and loose, which does more against rot than spraying can. Pull at veraison, when berries colour and soften, and the bunch is made: only its light changes.

`Q` **Half the bunches are cut off and left on the ground in July. What does a green harvest actually buy?**
  Mostly evenness: cutting away the bunches lagging behind leaves a crop that ripens together. Concentration is the part that disappoints, because berries thinned early swell to fill the space they are given. It is a late correction for a crop that pruning already set too high.

`Q` **Vineyards are sprayed with water all through a spring frost night. Why does sealing a bud in ice save it?**
  Water gives up heat as it freezes, and that holds the bud near zero while the air falls further. Candles warm the air instead, and wind machines pull warmer air down from above it. The spray has to run until the thaw: stop halfway and the ice takes heat back out and kills the bud.

`Q` **Machine harvesting is fast and cheap. What can it not do at all?**
  A harvester shakes fruit off the stems, so what arrives is loose berries and juice, never a bunch, and it takes everything it touches. Champagne bans it, and carbonic maceration and noble rot picking both need what it cannot give. It does work at night, in the cool.

`Q` **An old vineyard is described as a field blend. What does that fix about the wine?**
  The varieties are interplanted, so they come off on one day whether each is ready or not and go into one ferment. Nothing can be adjusted afterwards. It began as insurance rather than art: a year that ruined one variety usually spared another growing beside it.

### Washington

`Q` **Washington grows most of its wine in near-desert east of the Cascades, on eight inches of rain a year. How does that work?**
  Irrigation turns a liability into control. With almost no rain, a grower decides exactly when the vine gets water and when it goes short, which is a lever growers in wetter places do not have. The sandy soils also carry no phylloxera, so much of the state is ungrafted.

### Winemaking

`·` **Malolactic conversion always softens acidity. So why does it not always taste buttery?**
  It converts sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, raising pH. Diacetyl, the buttery compound, is only a by-product: the bacteria can metabolise it further, lees stirring disperses it, and blending dilutes it. Chablis, in northern Burgundy, routinely does MLF without tasting buttery.

`·` **What does a winemaker pay for including whole bunches in a red ferment?**
  Stems buy aromatic lift, firmer tannin and a cooler, slower ferment. They also absorb pigment, so the wine finishes paler, and they release potassium, which raises pH at the cost of acidity. Unripe stems add a green, stalky note that never leaves.

`·` **What is carbonic maceration doing that a normal red ferment is not?**
  Fermenting the grape from the inside. Whole uncrushed berries are sealed under carbon dioxide, and each one starts converting its own sugar with its own enzymes, before yeast ever reaches it. That builds banana and kirsch esters, and takes colour without much tannin.

`Q` **A white wine is left on its lees, the dead yeast left by fermentation, and stirred weekly. What does that buy?**
  Stirring the lees back through the wine. As the cells break down they release mannoproteins, which add weight and a creamy feel without any sugar. The lees also consume oxygen, so the wine is shielded. Overdone it buries the fruit. The French for the stirring is bâtonnage.

`·` **Nearly every wine has sulphur dioxide added. What is it actually doing?**
  Two jobs: it stuns spoilage microbes, and it protects the wine from oxidation. Only the free portion works, since the rest binds to other compounds and goes inert. That is why a lab reports free and total separately, and why the total on its own tells you little.

`Q` **A cheap young white smells loudly of pear drop and banana. Where was that aroma made?**
  Yeast builds acetate esters, and a cold ferment near 12–16C keeps far more of them in the wine. Isoamyl acetate is the pear drop and banana one. Those esters slowly come apart in bottle, so the smell is loudest in the first year and thin by the third.

`Q` **Why does a high-pH wine need a far bigger sulphur dose to be as well protected as a low-pH one?**
  Only a small share of a wine's free sulphur dioxide is molecular SO2, the uncharged form that stuns microbes, and pH sets that share steeply. Holding the same molecular level takes about four times the free sulphur at pH 3.6 as at the sharper pH 3.0, and the legal cap does not move.

`Q` **A back label says the wine had eighteen months of élevage. What was happening in that time?**
  Everything between the last of the fermentation and the bottling: which vessel, how long, how much air reaches the wine, when it is blended. Most of a wine's texture is settled in that stretch, so two lots off one ferment can arrive quite different. Élevage means raising.

`Q` **A back label says the wine is unfined and unfiltered. What two things were skipped?**
  Fining adds something that binds a target and sinks with it: clay for the proteins that haze a white, egg white for hard tannin in a red. Filtration strains instead. Both take a little texture and aroma too, so leaving them out buys weight and costs clarity and stability.

### Zinfandel

`Q` **Zinfandel routinely finishes above 15% and shows a raisined edge. What in the vineyard causes both?**
  One bunch holds raisins next to green fruit whatever day it is picked, so the grower is always choosing which fault to take. The raisined berries carry huge sugar and the yeast turns that into alcohol. Primitivo in Puglia is the same grape under an Italian name.

## tea (161)

### Altitude

`·` **Why is Taiwanese high-mountain oolong so much less astringent?**
  Above roughly 1000m, cooler temperatures and persistent cloud slow the plant's growth and reduce catechin production, while amino acids stay relatively higher. Catechins are the main source of astringency. The result reads thick and sweet rather than brisk.

### Anhui

`Q` **Taiping Houkui is a flat green tea with unusually long leaves, each marked with a faint criss-cross grid. What made that grid?**
  The leaf is laid out straight and rolled flat under a gauze mesh, which prints itself on. The flattening, with the local large-leaf bush, gives an orchid scent and very little astringency for leaves that mature. The leaves are long enough to brew upright in a tall glass.

`Q` **Lu'an Guapian is finished by swinging baskets of leaf over an open charcoal fire, dozens of passes in relays. What does that buy?**
  The basket crosses the blaze for a second at a time, so the leaf takes hard heat in flashes and never sits in it. That drives out the last water and lays a toasted sweetness on. The move is called pulling the old fire. It is the one famous Chinese green with no bud in it.

`Q` **Good Huangshan Maofeng shows a small pale leaf at the foot of each bud. What is it?**
  Every shoot opens with a fish leaf: a small rounded one that never grows on. A bud still carrying it was taken at the very start of the flush, so graders leave it in rather than sort it out. It is why the tea is pale, downy and orchid-scented rather than grassy.

### Assam

`·` **What does CTC do to the leaf, and why is most Assam made that way?**
  Crush, tear, curl: the leaf goes through toothed rollers that shred it into hard granules. Nearly every cell is broken, so oxidation is fast and complete and the brew is strong and dark in two minutes. It is built for milk, bags and one infusion, not for leaf grades.
