`Q` **Almost every famous tea region is a hillside, yet Assam is a hot river plain barely above sea level. Why does that work?**
  Assam is where tea's other variety grows wild. Large-leaf assamica was found in its forests in the 1820s, and until then Britain believed tea grew only in China. It wants monsoon heat and flood-plain damp, so altitude, the usual mark of fine tea, means nothing on an Assam pack.

`Q` **Assam's first flush is thin and its second flush is the one sold by name. What does late May bring that March does not?**
  The rains. Assam's March crop grows through a dry, cool spring and comes out light and brisk. The monsoon breaks in late May, and the large-leaf bush finally has the heat and water it is built for. That flush is the dark, malty tea with golden tips.

### Blending

`·` **Why does a supermarket black tea taste the same in June as it did in January?**
  Because it is built to. A blender tastes samples from many gardens and mixes to a fixed specification, then rewrites the recipe as the crops change so that the cup does not. A single-garden tea is the opposite bargain: it moves with the season, and that movement is what you bought.

`Q` **Masala chai is boiled with its spices rather than steeped like tea. What forces that method?**
  Different materials give up at different rates. Cardamom, cinnamon bark, ginger and clove hold their oils in woody tissue a three minute steep barely touches, so they need a rolling boil and time. The tea is picked to survive that, which is why it is usually hard CTC.

`Q` **A blender puts several different teas in one packet. Why do their leaf sizes usually match?**
  Surface area sets extraction speed. Put fine broken leaf beside whole leaf and the small is spent inside a minute, while the large is still opening. The cup keeps changing shape as it brews, so no single time is right for it. Blenders match the grade first, then the flavour.

`Q` **A blend that tastes right at home comes out thin and dull a few hundred miles away. What is likely different?**
  Blenders build to the water their customers actually have. A blend pitched for hard, alkaline water is made brisk and strong so the minerals have something to knock down. Brewed in soft water that same leaf reads harsh; a soft-water blend in hard water goes flat.

### Brewing

`·` **Why does gongfu brewing taste different from Western brewing of the same leaf?**
  It is a different extraction curve. A high leaf-to-water ratio with very short steeps pulls compounds out in stages, so you taste the tea evolve across infusions. A single long Western steep extracts most of it at once, averaging that whole progression into one cup.

`Q` **Why is gyokuro, a shaded Japanese green, brewed at around 60C when oolong takes boiling water?**
  Compounds do not all dissolve at the same temperature. Theanine and the other amino acids come out readily in cool water; catechins and caffeine need heat. Sixty degrees selects for sweetness and body. A tight oolong ball needs boiling water simply to open.

`Q` **Why keep one pot of Yixing clay, from the potting town in Jiangsu, for one kind of tea?**
  The clay is fired unglazed and stays slightly porous, so oil and aroma soak into the wall and return to the next brew. Thick clay holds heat too, which suits roasted oolong and puerh. A porcelain gaiwan, the lidded cup, gives nothing back, so tasters judge in one.

`Q` **Why is the second infusion of a rolled oolong usually the strongest?**
  The first steep of a tight ball only wets the outside, and the leaf is still shut. By the second it has unfurled, so the water reaches every surface at once and the brew peaks. After that each steep takes what is left, and the tea thins and sweetens as it goes.

`·` **A fine foam rises on the first infusion. Is something wrong with the tea?**
  No. The leaf carries saponins, natural foaming compounds that lower the water's surface tension, and a fast pour whips them up. Bud-heavy and freshly made teas throw the most of it. The old habit is to skim it off with the lid, but there is nothing in it to avoid.

`Q` **Two unglazed Yixing pots: one a fine red clay fired almost dense, one a coarse sandy clay left porous. What changes in the cup?**
  Density. Zhu ni, a fine red ore from the Yixing hills in Jiangsu, fires almost tight, so little soaks in and a fragrant oolong comes through loud. Duan ni is coarse and far more porous, so it absorbs more and rounds bitterness off, which suits raw puerh or a heavy roast.

`Q` **A small pitcher sits between the pot and the cups, and the pot is emptied into it before a single cup is filled. What is it for?**
  Tea leaving a pot runs weak at the start and strong at the last drops, so the pitcher blends the whole infusion to one strength. Draining the pot dry also stops the brewing, which is what lets an infusion be timed in seconds. It is the fairness cup, gong dao bei.

`Q` **Leaving a tea bag in longer makes the cup bitter rather than stronger. What is different about loose leaf?**
  A bag holds fannings and dust, the finest fractions sorted out of production, and their surface is so large that almost everything soluble is out inside a minute. After that only astringency climbs. Whole leaf gives up its parts in order, so time is still a lever there.

`Q` **Some teas are boiled in a pan rather than steeped in a pot. Which ones, and why?**
  Mature leaf and stalk are woody, and years under the press shut a cake tighter still, so five minutes in hot water takes very little out of either. A rolling boil pulls the sugars and the body through. It is how butter tea is made on the Tibetan plateau.

`Q` **Two brews of one leaf come out equally strong: more leaf briefly, or less leaf for longer. Do they taste alike?**
  Compounds leave the leaf at different rates. Amino acids and simple sugars come out early and then level off; catechins and caffeine keep climbing the longer the leaf sits. Matching strength with time buys the same intensity with more bitterness underneath it.

### Ceylon

`Q` **A Ceylon pack says high grown. What does that actually tell you?**
  Elevation, not rank. Sri Lanka splits its tea at 600m and 1200m. High grown, above 1200m, gives a pale, brisk, aromatic liquor. Low grown, under 600m, gives a dark, thick, heavy one that much of the Middle East prefers. Neither band is the better tea.

`Q` **Dimbula in Sri Lanka makes its best tea in January and February. What is happening then?**
  Sri Lanka takes two monsoons from opposite directions, so one flank of the central hills is soaked while the other has gone dry and windy. Dimbula faces west and peaks in January; the eastern slopes peak in July. A date on a Ceylon pack means little until you know which flank grew it.

### Chemistry

`Q` **Gyokuro, the most prized Japanese green, is shaded for weeks before picking. What does the shade actually change?**
  Theanine is made in the roots and sent up to the leaf, where light drives its conversion toward catechins, the bitter compounds, and drives catechin synthesis besides. Take the light away for about three weeks and theanine builds up instead. That is the brothy weight.

`Q` **Oxidation turns green leaf into black tea. What does it do to catechins, the leaf's bitter compounds?**
  Joins them up. Catechins pair off into theaflavins, which are orange, bright and brisk, and those link further into thearubigins, brown, soft and far more abundant, which carry the colour and the body. Stop the oxidation early for briskness, run it long for depth.

`Q` **Tea and coffee both deliver caffeine. Why does tea's tend to feel steadier?**
  Theanine, the amino acid behind tea's brothy sweetness, arrives in the same cup. Trials pairing the two do show steadier attention, though they dose far more theanine than a cup holds. Tea also simply carries less caffeine per cup, which is part of the answer.

`Q` **Wherever the tea bush sees a real winter, the spring picking costs the most. What is the plant doing that earns that?**
  Cold stops growth, and through the dormant months the bush banks sugars and amino acids in its roots and wood. The first flush is grown out of that store rather than out of the day's sunlight, so it comes up sweet and low in bitterness.

`Q` **Decaffeinated tea reads thin and hollow beside the same leaf with its caffeine still in. Why?**
  Caffeine is stripped with carbon dioxide under pressure or with a solvent, and none of them can tell it from the polyphenols and aromatics beside it. Ethyl acetate is the cheap route and costs the most flavour, and naturally decaffeinated on a box means that solvent, not water.

`Q` **Crush a fresh tea leaf and it smells of cut grass within seconds. What has just been made?**
  Damage lets an enzyme reach the leaf's own fats and cut them into hexenal and hexenol within seconds. Those green leaf volatiles are the smell of any cut plant, not of tea. A long wither lets most of them disperse and convert, which is why under-withered tea reads raw and grassy.

`Q` **A tea is roasted and comes out smelling of nuts, cocoa and toast. Where did those smells come from?**
  Pyrazines, a family of nitrogen compounds that heat builds out of the leaf's own amino acids and sugars. They are made rather than uncovered, which is why roasting smells of nuts and cocoa whatever went in, and why a heavy fire can bury a plain leaf.

`Q` **White tea is sold as the gentle, low-caffeine one. Is it?**
  Caffeine is the plant's own insecticide and it is concentrated in the youngest growth, so a bud-only Silver Needle can carry more than a coarse black tea. The class tells you almost nothing. Leaf age, cultivar, water temperature and steep length are what decide the cup.

`Q` **A quick first steep is poured away to cut the caffeine. Roughly how much does that take out?**
  Caffeine comes out early but nowhere near completely. Estimates for a rinse of a few seconds up to half a minute run from under a tenth to about a fifth, and none is a direct measurement. Losing half needs minutes of steeping thrown away, and the flavour goes too.

### Classification

`Q` **What decides which of the six classes a Chinese tea belongs to?**
  Processing alone. Green, yellow, white, oolong, red and dark all come from the same plant. Note the vocabulary too: what English calls black tea is hong cha, red tea, and dark tea is a separate class, the one that holds puerh and the other hei cha.

### Cultivar

`Q` **If every tea is one species, what does a cultivar name tell you?**
  One species, sharply different clones. Var. assamica has large leaves and more polyphenol, var. sinensis is smaller and finer, and named cultivars go further still: Rou Gui, Qing Xin, Yabukita. Japan plants roughly 70% Yabukita, which narrows a whole country's flavour.

`·` **Why is almost all modern tea planted from cuttings rather than grown from seed?**
  The plant will not fertilise itself, so every seed is a cross and every seedling comes out different. A cutting is a clone, so a field ripens and tastes alike, and a cultivar name, which is just that clone's name, means something. Old seed-grown gardens are uneven, and valued for it.

### Dancong

`·` **Phoenix Dancong, from the Fenghuang mountains in Guangdong, is sold by aroma name. Is anything added to make it smell that way?**
  No. The names translate the smell: Mi Lan Xiang is honey orchid, Ya Shi Xiang is duck shit, and each is its own cultivar line off Fenghuang Shui Xian. Dan cong means single bush: the aromas were found on individual old trees, then propagated by cutting.

### Darjeeling

`·` **Darjeeling is sold by flush. What is a flush, and why do the first two taste nothing alike?**
  A flush is one growth cycle of the bush. First flush, from March, is barely oxidised and reads green and floral, closer to an oolong. Second flush, in May and June, is fully oxidised and gives the grapey muscatel note. Same bushes, different season, different making.

`Q` **Darjeeling tastes nothing like the tea grown on the plains below it. What is planted on those slopes?**
  Darjeeling was planted from Chinese seed while the plains were planted with the large-leaf Assam variety. The small-leaf plant grows slowly between 600m and 2000m and crops very little, which is much of why Darjeeling costs what it does and reads floral rather than heavy.

`Q` **A Darjeeling pack names the garden, then reads DJ-12, 2025. What is that number?**
  Gardens sell by invoice, and DJ is simply Darjeeling. A day's leaf off one section becomes a few chests, numbered in order from the season's start, so DJ-12 is early. It is a date stamp and not a score: a later lot off better weather can beat it.

### Dark tea

`·` **A brick of Hunan dark tea is speckled with gold. What is that?**
  A fungus, grown into the brick on purpose. The tea is pressed loose enough to breathe, then held warm and damp until it blooms right through. It softens coarse leaf and gives Fu brick its sweet, mushroomy smell. The name is golden flowers, and puerh is not the only dark tea.

`Q` **A shop offers you a dark tea called Liu Bao. What are you being sold?**
  Liu Bao comes from Wuzhou in Guangxi, not Yunnan. It is wet piled to ferment, then aged for years in huge breathing bamboo baskets. Cultivar, that pile and the long ageing together build binglang xiang, betel nut fragrance: cooling, medicinal, faintly sweet.

`·` **Anhua in Hunan presses dark tea into a log as tall as a man. How is that log actually built?**
  Steamed leaf is packed into a woven bamboo tube lined with leaves, then squeezed down its length with poles until it is solid, near 36kg. The damp casing shrinks as it dries and keeps tightening it. The log stands outdoors in sun and dew, and reaches you sawn into discs.

`Q` **A brick of Chinese dark tea is full of stalk and coarse old leaf that any other class would sort out. Why is it left in?**
  The microbes need it. Coarse leaf and stem hold the sugars and fibre that the fungi and bacteria of a dark tea pile actually feed on. So the grade is a specification, not a corner cut. Tender buds would starve the process. A Fu brick may legally run near a fifth stalk.

### Evaluation

`Q` **Chinese tea grading scores five things and adds them up. Why is an oolong not scored the same way as a green tea?**
  The weights move. Appearance, liquor colour, aroma, taste and leaf base are each scored, then multiplied: roughly 25/10/25/30/10 for green tea, 20/5/30/35/5 for oolong. Aroma and taste carry 65% of an oolong because that is what the category is for.

`Q` **A Chinese evaluator smells the same tea three times as it cools. What does each pass catch?**
  Volatiles leave at different temperatures, so one sniff reads one fraction. Hot brings the top notes and any scorching; warm gives the tea's own character at its fullest; cool shows what persists, and the staleness or muddiness that heat was covering.

`Q` **The Chinese standard judges green tea on one five-minute steep and oolong on three. Why the difference?**
  Endurance is part of the grade. Five grams sit in a 110ml covered bowl and are poured at roughly one, one and a half and two minutes, and the tea is reassessed after each. A tea that is loud once and hollow by the third pour has told the grader something.

`Q` **A grader spreads the brewed leaf out, looks at it, then presses it between finger and thumb. What is the pressing for?**
  Leaf base is a scored factor and it is read by touch as well as by eye. Soft and springy says tender leaf, handled well; brittle or hard says over-firing or coarse material. Colour at the margin says how far oxidation ran. Western cupping rarely scores any of it.

`Q` **China holds tea people to two separate professional standards rather than one ladder. What splits them?**
  Two trades, two exams. The evaluator scores a tea against a written standard: appearance, liquor, aroma, taste, leaf base. The tea-art practitioner is examined on ceremony, ware, the tea table and service. Western sommelier courses fold a thin version of both into one.

### Faults

`Q` **A green tea that tasted clean in the shop is sour and hay-like a month later. What most likely went wrong?**
  The last drying is what makes tea shelf-stable. It takes the leaf to roughly 2–3% moisture and shuts the chemistry down. Left wetter than that, the leaf keeps oxidising inside the packet and can grow mould. Green tea shows it first, because nothing in it was meant to change.

`Q` **A tea bought loose from an open jar in a shop tastes faintly of that shop once you get it home. What has happened to it?**
  Dry tea is porous and coated in its own oils, and it takes up the smells around it within days. That is exactly the property jasmine scenting uses on purpose. So keep tea away from spices, coffee and a shared fridge, and be wary of an open jar.

`Q` **A dark tea brick shows fungal growth through it. What separates the wanted kind from the ruinous kind?**
  Three things together. Golden flowers are one specific fungus, deliberately grown under held warmth and damp, and appear as small firm gold granules right through the brick. Spoilage mould is uninvited, fuzzy, white, green or black, smells musty, and carries a real toxin risk.

### Food

`Q` **Why does milk soften a strong black tea?**
  Astringency is polyphenols binding the proteins in your saliva and stripping the mouth dry. Milk brings its own protein, which binds them first, so less of that grip ever reaches you. The same trade is why a fatty dish softens a brisk tea and why dark tea suits rich meat.

`Q` **Milk suits a strong Assam and wrecks a jasmine green. What is it doing to the delicate tea?**
  Fat traps the aroma. Most of what a scented tea smells of is oil soluble, so milk fat takes those compounds into itself and far less reaches the air above the cup. A strong black tea still has colour, body and grip left. A perfumed one is mostly the perfume.

`Q` **A pinch of salt takes the bitterness out of a tea that brewed too hard. What is it doing?**
  Sodium interferes with the way bitterness is registered. So it takes bitterness away rather than covering it over, and it works well below the level at which you would taste salt at all. Cooks use the same trick on grapefruit and on coffee.

`Q` **Wherever tea is drunk heavily sweetened it is also brewed unusually strong. Why do those two habits travel together?**
  Sugar dissolved in the tea itself suppresses both bitterness and the dry grip of astringency, which lifts the ceiling on how hard the leaf can be pushed. Moroccan mint tea, masala chai and Turkish tea are all built on that trade.

`Q` **A sushi counter serves a big mug of coarse, scalding green tea at the end of the meal and never the good leaf. What is that tea for?**
  It is deliberately coarse: the dust sorted out of sencha during refining, brewed scalding. Fat sets on a cool mouth and a hot drying liquor clears it, which is the job. A delicate tea would be lost against soy and vinegar anyway. The tea is agari, the dust konacha.

### Grading

`·` **Shincha, sencha, bancha, kukicha: what do those names actually describe?**
  When it was picked and which part of the plant it is, not a quality ladder. Shincha is the first flush of the year, sencha the standard rolled leaf, bancha a later and coarser picking, kukicha the stems sorted out during refining. Cheaper, and a different thing.

`Q` **A Darjeeling tin is stamped FTGFOP. What is that grading?**
  The leaf, not the liquor. The letters stack up a description: Orange Pekoe is a whole-leaf grade, and flowery, golden, tippy and finest each claim more bud or better appearance. None of it is a tasting score, and a broken grade can still brew the better cup.

### Green tea

`·` **Why does Chinese green tea taste nutty while Japanese green tea tastes marine?**
  The fixing method. China pan-fires, which introduces Maillard character: chestnut, toast, a rounder body. Japan steams, which halts oxidation faster and preserves more chlorophyll, producing the vivid green, grassy, oceanic profile of sencha and gyokuro.

`Q` **Two senchas come from one field and one was steamed far longer. Which is it?**
  Deep steaming, fukamushi, runs a minute or more against roughly thirty seconds for light. The extra heat breaks the leaf apart, so fine particles cloud the cup, extraction is fast and sweet, astringency drops, and the aroma is quieter and keeps less well.

`·` **Matcha is ground leaf. What leaf, exactly, goes into the mill?**
  Tencha. It is shaded like gyokuro and steamed like sencha, but it is never rolled, and the stems and veins are cut out before it dries flat. Rolling exists to shape leaf for infusing, and matcha is not infused, so the leaf goes to a stone mill whole.

`·` **Anji Bai Cha, from Anji county in Zhejiang, translates as Anji white tea, yet it is a green tea. Why the name?**
  The leaf, not the class. Its Bai Ye No.1 bush turns albino in a narrow band around 20C. Early spring shoots come out pale jade with green veins, and stack amino acids where polyphenols would normally go. Warmer or colder it greens over, so the picking window is short.

`·` **Longjing leaf lies flat and smooth rather than curled or twisted. What made it that shape?**
  The pressing. A hand holds the leaf flat against the hot wok as it fires. So three jobs happen at once: the heat kills the enzymes, the leaf dries, and the shape is set. Elsewhere those are three separate stages. It goes into the wok twice, with a rest between.

`Q` **Biluochun is a tiny spiral green tea from the hills above Lake Tai, west of Suzhou in Jiangsu. Why are its bushes planted in among fruit trees?**
  For the blossom, by tradition. Apricot, plum, peach and loquat stand among the tea on the lake's Dongting hills, and the local account is that the leaf takes their scent up as it grows. Picked tiny and thick with down, it scorches, so brew it under 80C.

`Q` **Enshi Yulu in Hubei is steamed rather than fired in a pan, which almost no other Chinese green tea is. Why does it stand alone?**
  Steaming is how the Tang fixed green tea. Japan took the method and kept it, while China turned to the wok. Enshi Yulu is the one steamed Chinese green made at any scale, and it arrives as a dark jade needle, drinking closer to a sencha than to its neighbours.

`Q` **A Chinese green tea is sold as ming qian, picked before the Qingming festival around 4 April. Why is that date worth less than it looks?**
  Qingming is a calendar date and the bush does not know it. A warm southern lowland garden is well into its flush by then, and a high cold one may not have moved at all. The words rank pickings within one garden and mean very little across two.

### Japan

`·` **Hojicha is roasted brown and is drunk in the evening. Is the roasting what makes it low in caffeine?**
  Only partly. Roasting at 150–200C drives some off, but most of it is the raw material: hojicha is made from bancha, the coarse late leaf, and from stems, both low in caffeine already. Genmaicha gets there differently, cutting the leaf with its own volume of roasted rice.

`Q` **Sencha, kabusecha and gyokuro can be made from one field. What separates them?**
  Shade, applied as two dials: how long, and how heavy. Sencha gets none. Kabusecha is covered for roughly a week to ten days, often with cloth laid straight over the bushes. Gyokuro runs twenty days or more under denser cover, so it goes furthest toward sweet and brothy.

`Q` **Japanese green tea leaves the farm as aracha, crude leaf still full of stem and dust. What does a refiner do to it?**
  A refining house sorts out the stem and dust, then fires the leaf again: hi-ire, the finishing fire. How hard it fires is a house decision, so one field can reach you smelling of toasted nuts or of cut grass. Shincha is deliberately fired lightest.

`Q` **Nearly all Japanese green tea is steamed. What is done differently to kamairicha?**
  It is pan-fired instead of steamed. The leaf tumbles in the drum rather than passing through the rollers that straighten sencha into needles, so it comes out curled and loose. Kyushu makes nearly all of it, and that curl in the packet gives it away.

`Q` **Why does the first Japanese green tea of the year nearly always come from Kagoshima rather than from Uji?**
  Spring arrives there first, and the fields are flat enough to plant early cultivars and cut them by machine. Uji sits far to the north on slopes and follows two or three weeks later, with Shizuoka further east again the biggest grower. A first tea tells you where it grew.

`Q` **A Japanese tea farm plants Saemidori and Okumidori in among its Yabukita. What is that mixture for?**
  Fresh leaf has to be steamed the day it is cut, so a field that comes ready all at once is more than a farm can handle. Saemidori buds about five days early and Okumidori some ten days late, so the harvest runs over weeks. The late one dodges frost as well.

`Q` **The tea year in Japan's tea ceremony opens in November, with leaf that was picked the previous May. Where has it been?**
  The leaf matcha is ground from goes whole into a sealed jar in spring and is opened in November, and only then milled. Six months shut away rounds the sharpness off. It rests whole because ground matcha only goes stale. Cutting that seal opens the tea year: kuchikiri.

`Q` **A tin says Uji tea. How much does that name promise about where the leaf grew?**
  The Kyoto trade defines Uji tea as leaf grown in Kyoto, Nara, Shiga or Mie and then refined inside Kyoto: sorted, blended and fired by a Kyoto house. Uji itself is small and largely built over. The name promises the finishing hand rather than the field.

### Keemun

`Q` **Keemun is Anhui's famous black tea, from a district that had made only green tea for centuries. Where did it come from?**
  It was made on purpose, for export. A Qimen man learned black tea making in Fujian and brought it home in the 1870s, because Europe wanted black tea and the district's green was not selling. Which man is disputed. Its cultivar is heavy in geraniol, so the cup reads rose-like.

### Kenya

`·` **Darjeeling and Assam are sold by flush. Why is Kenyan tea never sold that way?**
  It grows on the equator at 1500–2700m, so there is no winter and the bush never goes dormant. Leaf comes off every week or two all year, which leaves no first or second flush to name. Kenya is the largest exporter of black tea in the world and nearly all of it goes into blends.

`Q` **Most Kenyan tea comes off farms of an acre or two rather than estates. What does that do to how it is judged?**
  Smallholders deliver green leaf to a shared factory within hours of picking, so hundreds of farms become one batch. The factory, not the farm, is what a buyer names and judges, and quality moves with processing rather than with any one garden.

### Matcha

`Q` **Why does matcha go stale in weeks when leaf tea keeps for a year?**
  Every particle is a freshly cut face. Milled to a few microns, the leaf meets far more oxygen and light than a rolled needle does. The vivid green dulls toward khaki and the sweetness gives way to hay. Buy small tins, and keep them cold and sealed.

`Q` **Usucha, thin tea, and koicha, thick tea, come from the same tin of matcha. What actually changes?**
  Roughly 2g of powder whisked into 70ml gives usucha, foamed and light. Koicha is about double the powder in half the water, stirred slowly to a smooth paste rather than beaten. Nothing bitter survives that concentration, so koicha uses only top grades.

`·` **A tin says ceremonial grade matcha. What has that phrase been checked against?**
  Nothing. No Japanese body defines it and no rule restricts it; it was coined for export buyers. Harvest, shade and mill decide the powder. Ask for first-flush leaf and stone grinding, then judge the tin: bright jade rather than khaki, and no grit between the fingers.

### Myanmar

`Q` **In Myanmar tea is eaten as well as drunk. What has been done to the leaf on the plate?**
  Laphet is pickled. Steamed leaf is pressed hard into a pit or a bamboo tube to shut the air out. Lactic bacteria and yeasts then sour it over months, the way they sour cabbage. It reaches the table savoury and tart, with fried beans, garlic and sesame.

### Nepal

`Q` **Ilam in eastern Nepal sits on the same ridges as Darjeeling and can taste remarkably like it. What is the real difference?**
  A protected name, not a break in the geology. Darjeeling's is legally defined and closed to leaf from outside it, and Nepal has no equivalent. So very similar tea off the same ridge sells for less, and much of it leaves the country anonymously into blends.

### Nilgiri

`Q` **Iced tea blends are built on Nilgiri from southern India. What is that leaf chosen for?**
  Creaming down. As black tea cools, its caffeine and tannin lock together and drop out, which clouds the cup. The stronger the liquor, the more of it. It is not a fault. Nilgiri, from the hills of Tamil Nadu, brews light, creams little, and pours clear over ice.

### Oolong

`·` **What does the word oolong actually specify?**
  A processing range, not a plant and not a place. Oxidation spans roughly 20–80%, the widest of any category. Anxi tieguanyin, from southern Fujian, sits near 20% and close to green tea; Wuyi yancha, northern Fujian, runs 50–70% plus charcoal roast and sits close to black.

`Q` **Oolong is sold as 20, 40 or 70 percent oxidised. What is that percentage a measurement of?**
  It is a convention rather than a reading. No maker measures the leaf in the moment; the figure is judged from the colour of the bruised margin, the smell and the feel, then passed on by habit. Two makers can call one tea 30% and 50%, so treat it as a style marker.

`Q` **Unrolled oolong leaf comes out green in the middle with a red rim. What did that?**
  Tossing the leaf in baskets or drums, resting it, and repeating that for hours. The tumbling bruises the margins and only the margins, so oxidation runs at the edge while the centre stays green. That is how oolong lands on a percentage instead of a switch. The step is yao qing.

`·` **How does a loose oolong leaf end up as a hard little ball?**
  Warm leaf is packed into a cloth bag, twisted into a ball and pressed under a machine. Then it is tipped out, broken up and reheated, and the cycle runs again. It repeats for hours. Empty a spent pot and the leaves unfold whole. The step is cloth rolling, tuan rou.

`·` **A charcoal-roasted oolong costs several times what the same leaf roasted in an oven does. What is being paid for?**
  Labour, mostly. Charcoal is a bed of embers under ash beneath a bamboo basket, radiating low heat for hours and repeated over months, and someone has to tend it. An oven holds a set temperature exactly and cheaply. Makers hold that the slow fire sinks deeper.

`·` **Why does an oolong maker watch the sky more anxiously than a green tea maker?**
  Oolong opens with shai qing, sun withering: the leaf is spread outdoors for a short spell to soften and start its aroma chemistry, then carried in to cool and rest before the tossing begins. Cloud or rain forces it inside under fans and the tea comes out duller.

### Plucking

`·` **Bud-only plucking is the finest grade, so why is oolong not picked that way?**
  Different job. A bud is rich in theanine and caffeine, which suits a delicate green or a silver needle. Oolong wants kai mian cai, open-face picking of three or four mature leaves, because mature leaf holds the aroma precursors and survives long rolling and roasting.

`Q` **A garden stops plucking for a fortnight in the middle of the season. What is the bush doing?**
  Shoots grow in bursts rather than steadily. After a few leaves the tip sets a banjhi, a blind bud that makes no new leaf, and the shoot stalls until the stem below widens enough to feed it. Pluckers wait out that pause, and it is what puts gaps between pickings.

`Q` **A tea garden is a flat hedge clipped to waist height. What is plucking itself doing to the plant?**
  Plucking is pruning. Apical dominance means a growing tip holds the buds below it asleep, so taking the tip wakes them and the bush answers with more shoots than it lost. That is why tea is a hedge and not the tree it would be, and why the table is cut back every few years.

### Processing

`·` **What is the difference between oxidation and roasting?**
  Oxidation is enzymatic and happens to the fresh leaf: it is the process that turns green tea into black. Roasting is applied heat after processing is finished: it caramelises sugars and drives off moisture, and it can be repeated years later to revive a stored tea.

`·` **What is withering actually for?**
  Controlled moisture loss. It makes the leaf pliable enough to roll without shattering, and it starts the chemical changes that precede oxidation. Under-withered leaf breaks up during processing; over-withered leaf loses aromatic potential before it is even rolled.

`Q` **Kill-green is the burst of heat that shuts down the enzymes that would otherwise brown fresh leaf. Why is it a dial rather than a switch?**
  Heat denatures the enzymes that drive oxidation, and how far it goes is a choice. Green tea is fixed hard, so nothing is left to change and it can only fade. Puerh's maocha, its unpressed loose leaf, is fixed gently and sun-dried, leaving enzyme and surface microbes intact for decades.

`·` **What is rolling for, if the leaf is going to be oxidised anyway?**
  It ruptures the cells so the enzymes and the compounds they act on finally meet, which is what lets oxidation run at all. It also sets the shape, and shape sets extraction: a tight ball opens over many infusions where broken leaf gives everything at once.

`Q` **A heavily roasted oolong tastes harsh and ashy the week it is made. What fixes it?**
  Time in the jar. Charcoal-roasted oolong is rested for weeks or months, tui huo, letting the fire retreat: moisture redistributes through the leaf and the char note sinks back under the tea. A heavy roast can want a year. Buying one straight off the fire is buying it early.

`Q` **GABA tea is neither a plant nor a place. What is done to the leaf?**
  With no air to work with, the leaf turns anaerobic and converts its glutamic acid into GABA, a nerve signalling compound the body also makes itself. A Japanese researcher, Tsushida, found the trick in 1987. Taiwan makes most of it now, and it carries a sour, stewed-fruit note.

`Q` **Rolled black tea leaf is set aside to oxidise. What is the maker controlling while it does?**
  Oxidation gives off its own heat, so a deep bed cooks itself. The leaf goes into a cool, damp room in thin layers for an hour or two. The maker reads the colour and the smell, then fires it hard to stop it. Run too warm and the tea comes out flat and stewed.

`Q` **A pack of Indian black tea says orthodox. What is that word describing?**
  Orthodox names the machine, not the garden. Rollers twist and press whole leaf the way hands once did, and how hard they press is a dial: light for a floral Darjeeling, hard for a strong Assam. One batch comes off in many sizes and is sifted into grades.

### Puerh

`·` **How do sheng and shou puerh differ?**
  Not by age. By process. Sheng is pressed raw and transforms slowly over decades. Shou was developed in the 1970s to imitate that result using 45–60 days of wet piling, wo dui, an accelerated microbial fermentation. Five-year examples of each have very little in common.

`·` **Black tea is often called fully fermented. Why is that the wrong word?**
  Nothing microbial happens to it. Black tea is oxidised: the leaf's own enzymes react with its polyphenols in air, the chemistry that browns a cut apple. Real fermentation, microbes and all, belongs to the dark teas, and shou puerh's wet piling is the clearest case.

`Q` **Two raw puerh cakes, same year and same processing, one Yiwu and one Bulang. How do they differ?**
  Origin. Both are mountains in Xishuangbanna, southern Yunnan. Yiwu, east of the Mekong, gives a gentle, thick, honeyed tea; Bulang, west of it, is known for a bitterness that turns into huigan, the sweetness that floods back after you swallow. Lao Ban Zhang is Bulang's costliest village.

`·` **What do gushu and taidi mean on a puerh label?**
  Old tree and terrace. Gushu is leaf from old seed-grown trees standing in mixed forest; taidi is plantation tea, cloned, hedged low and picked often. Deep roots and small crops make gushu thicker and longer in the cup. Far more is sold as gushu than can exist.

`Q` **A twenty-year-old raw puerh and a young cake pushed hard in damp storage both pour dark. What separates them in the cup?**
  Age softens a tea without emptying it. A well-kept old cake still has grip and a sweetness that returns after you swallow, with camphor, dried plum and old wood behind it. Damp storage buys the colour in a couple of years and leaves a musty note that never brews out.

`·` **A puerh wrapper reads 7542 and gives no other name. What are those four digits saying?**
  A blending recipe. The first two digits are the year the recipe was written, 1975 here, the third the leaf grade with higher meaning coarser, the fourth the factory, all in Yunnan: 1 Kunming, 2 Menghai, 3 Xiaguan. Standardised in 1976. The year is the recipe's, not the tea's.

`Q` **Laos and Myanmar grow the same big-leaf tea and press it the same way. Why is none of it puerh?**
  China's 2008 standard makes puerh a geographical indication, a name tied to a place: Yunnan large-leaf assamica, taken to sun-dried loose leaf and processed inside a listed set of Yunnan counties. Leaf crosses those borders constantly and is pressed anyway, so a wrapper is a claim.

`Q` **Large flat yellowish leaves are picked out of loose puerh leaf before it is pressed into a cake. Why are they rejected?**
  The oldest leaf on the shoot, too stiff to twist up when the batch is rolled, so it stays flat and pale and is sorted out. Pressed and sold on its own it is cheap, and being mature leaf it is sweeter and lower in caffeine, so it forgives a long steep. Yellow flakes, huang pian.

`Q` **Why does a puerh cake's outer leaf often look better than what a pick pulls out of the middle?**
  Some cakes are faced. A layer of better leaf goes into the mould before the body follows, so the surface is not a sample of the whole. That is why buyers pry from a broken edge rather than the face, and why a serious seller will hand you a cake already opened.

### Scenting

`Q` **How does jasmine tea get its scent?**
  By absorption, repeated. Jasmine opens and releases its scent after dark, so the flowers are layered warm through the tea overnight, taken out, and replaced with fresh ones for up to nine rounds. Earl Grey is the other method: bergamot, a bitter citrus, applied to the leaf as an oil.

`Q` **A good jasmine tea carries a heavy, almost animal weight under the flowers. What is that?**
  Indole, one of jasmine's own compounds. On its own it smells faecal; in traces it gives the heady depth beneath the flowers. Tea flavoured with jasmine oil tends to carry the sweet top note and none of that weight, so it comes across clean, loud and thin.

### Storage

`·` **Which tea should not be stored airtight, and why?**
  Sheng puerh. Green, white and oolong all degrade with oxygen, light and humidity, so they want a seal. Sheng needs modest airflow and humidity for its microbial and oxidative ageing to proceed at all. Sealed away, it simply stalls.

`Q` **The same sheng cake is stored in Kunming and in Guangzhou. Which one changes faster?**
  Humidity sets the rate. Guangzhou, on the subtropical south coast, sits above 80% much of the year, and a cake there darkens and softens in years rather than decades. Kunming, high in Yunnan, is cool and dry, so change is slow and clean. Push too far and you get mould.

`·` **Puerh is pressed into cakes. What does that do besides making it easy to carry?**
  It slows the ageing and makes it even. Only the outside of a cake meets much air, so the whole piece changes together and more slowly than loose leaf, which ages faster and less evenly. Press it harder and it slows further: an iron-pressed cake outlasts a stone-pressed one.

`Q` **Green tea and light oolong keep for a year or more in a freezer. What ruins them on the way out?**
  Cold slows the oxidation that dulls green leaf, and Japan and Taiwan freeze stock as a matter of course. The danger is on the way out: a cold pack opened in a warm kitchen pulls water straight onto bone-dry leaf. Let it reach room temperature before the seal is broken.

`Q` **A jar of roasted oolong laid down for ten years gets re-roasted every year or two. What is that maintenance for?**
  Leaf pulls water out of the air, and past a few percent it turns soft and grassy again, which sellers call fan qing, returning to green. A light re-firing drives that water back out. Aged oolong is tended, not left alone, and a heavier first roast buys longer gaps.

### Taiwan

`Q` **Oriental Beauty is made from leaf that insects have already chewed. Why is that wanted?**
  The tea green leafhopper feeds on the young shoots and the plant answers chemically. Monoterpenes rise, the family behind muscat grapes and Darjeeling's muscatel note, and other compounds bring the honey. It is a wound response, so the field cannot be sprayed and yields fall.

`Q` **A Taiwanese oolong is sold as Baozhong, Dong Ding, Alishan or Lishan. What does that name tell you?**
  Elevation, mostly. Baozhong comes from Pinglin at 400–800m, barely oxidised and left in loose twists rather than rolled into balls. Dong Ding sits at 600–800m and is traditionally roasted. Alishan begins around 1000m, Lishan at 1600m and above.

`Q` **Taiwanese competition tea is judged from one fixed brew. What does that do to the winning style?**
  Three grams sit in 150ml of boiling water for six minutes, blind, with taste and aroma carrying most of the score. Six minutes is far longer than anyone drinks, so any harshness is dragged into the cup. A winner is a tea with nothing to hide, which is not the same as the best one to drink.

`Q` **Where does the creamy smell in a Taiwanese milk oolong come from?**
  Jin Xuan was bred in Taiwan in 1981 and carries lactones that read as cream, so lightly oxidised it comes out milky on its own. Much of what is exported as milk oolong is that cultivar sprayed with flavouring, which is louder and holds through every steep.

`Q` **Sun Moon Lake's Ruby 18 is a black tea that finishes cool and minty with nothing added to it. Where does that come from?**
  A bred cultivar. It was crossed at a government station from a large-leaf Burmese plant and a wild Taiwanese mountain tea. The cool note comes down from that wild parent every harvest. Japan planted large-leaf tea at the lake in the 1920s, which is why black tea is made there.

`Q` **A Taiwanese oolong is offered as dong pian, and the seller says there was none at all last year. What is it?**
  Winter sprout. Above 1000m the bush shuts down after the November picking, but a mild December can trick it into pushing one more flush, cut before the spring crop. Some years it comes and some it does not, so dong pian is a one-off rather than a grade.

`Q` **A Taiwanese oolong is sold as gaoshan, high mountain. Is there a height it has to clear?**
  Gaoshan is a market word with no legal floor under it, and 1000m is convention rather than rule. Height is a stand-in for cloud, cold nights and slow growth, and a stand-in can be wrong: a cool shaded site below the line can beat a bare sunny one above it.

### Tasting

`·` **After a bitter, astringent tea, two separate things happen in the mouth. What are they?**
  Two halves of one aftertaste. The mouth waters back after the tea has dried it, which is sheng jin, generating fluid. Then a sweetness rises in the throat as the bitterness fades: hui gan, returning sweetness. Bitterness is the trigger, not a fault.

`·` **Why do tasters smell the dry leaf, then the wet leaf, then the liquor separately?**
  Because the aromatics leave in order of how volatile they are, which roughly tracks their weight. The lightest come off the hot wet leaf in the first seconds, which is why the lid goes straight under the nose. Heavier ones stay dissolved in the cup.

`Q` **A taster tips the brewed leaf out of the pot and spreads it on the lid. What is being read off it?**
  Brewing destroys the dry leaf's evidence and exposes the rest. Spread out wet, a hand pluck shows whole leaves on a torn stalk; a machine cut shows straight severed edges and stray old leaf. Colour at the rim says how far oxidation ran, and brittleness says how hard it was fired.

`Q` **A broker calls a black tea brisk. What is being described?**
  Brisk is a texture word, not a strength or a colour one: the clean lively grip that makes a cup refreshing and lets it carry milk. Its opposites in the trade are flat and soft. Beside it sit body, for weight in the mouth, and bright, for a clear live colour rather than a dull one.

`Q` **A taster calls one tea strong but thin and the next light but thick. Is that a contradiction?**
  Concentration is set by the brewer with leaf, water and time. The weight and coating a liquor has in the mouth is not, and comes largely from soluble sugars and polysaccharides the leaf built. Chinese tasters keep the words apart: nong for strong, hou for thick.

`Q` **In Taiwan a tall narrow cup is set beside the drinking cup and you are told not to drink from it. What is it for?**
  Tea is poured in, the drinking cup inverted over it and the pair turned so the tall one drains. What is left is a warm film with a lot of surface and no liquid holding it back, so it reads loud and keeps shifting for a minute. It is the aroma cup, wen xiang bei.

`Q` **Tasters let a cup go cold before they decide on a tea. What does cooling expose?**
  Sweetness falls away far faster than bitterness and grip do as a cup cools, and the aromatics that were lifting off the hot liquor stop arriving. A cold cup is the tea with its flattery removed, and one still sweet cold has something real underneath.

### Terroir

`·` **What is yan yun, and what is it attributed to?**
  Rock rhyme: the mineral signature of Wuyi yancha, off the cliffs of northern Fujian. It is credited to the weathered volcanic and sandstone soils of the narrow ravines, with sharp drainage and little direct sun. Zhengyan, true cliff tea, costs many times the flat-land tea.

`Q` **Turkey and Georgia grow tea further north than anywhere else. What lets the plant survive there?**
  Cold tolerance belongs to the plant. Small-leaf sinensis survives winters down to around minus 10C; big-leaf assamica, the tropical variety behind Assam and puerh, does not. That split draws the tea map, so a big broad leaf in the pot grew without a real winter.

### Tieguanyin

`·` **Is the jade-green, intensely floral style of tieguanyin, Anxi's famous oolong, the traditional one?**
  No. It is a market development from around the 1990s. Traditional tieguanyin, from Anxi in southern Fujian, was more oxidised, near 40%, and roasted. Demand for green, aromatic oolong pushed producers to 15–30% oxidation with little or no roast. Both are true to their era.

`Q` **A bag from Muzha in Taipei is labelled tieguanyin. What might that word be describing?**
  It names a cultivar and a way of making tea at once. Zhang Naimiao carried tieguanyin cuttings from Anxi to Muzha in 1895 and the heavy repeated charcoal roast came with them. Other bushes made that way sell under the name, so zheng cong, true bush, marks the original.

`·` **One oolong tin from Anxi in Fujian is marked qing xiang and the next nong xiang. What is that pair of words sorting?**
  How far the leaf was baked. Qing xiang, light aroma, is barely fired and stays green and floral. Nong xiang, dense aroma, is baked on and comes out amber, nutty and rounder. Chen xiang, aged aroma, is the third. They are national standard types, not shop language.

`Q` **Tossing bruises an oolong's leaf margins, so the spent leaf shows a red rim round a green centre. Why does a modern jade tieguanyin show almost none?**
  Once heat has stopped the leaf's enzymes the batch is wrapped in cloth and beaten. The oxidised margins dried hardest, so they shatter and fall away. Anxi in southern Fujian added the step for a brisker cup, and it hides how far oxidation ran. Removing the red edge.

### Tisane

`Q` **Chrysanthemum, kuding and roasted barley are all sold as cha. What do they share with tea, chemically?**
  Only the hot water. They come from unrelated families and carry none of tea's defining chemistry, so nothing you know about steeping tea transfers reliably. Each has its own extraction rate, its own kind of bitterness, and its own ways of going wrong.

`Q` **Chrysanthemum is drunk alongside shou puerh far more often than on its own. What does the pairing do?**
  Contrast. Shou puerh is thick, earthy and short on aromatic lift; chrysanthemum brings a clean floral top note and a little sweetness with almost no body of its own. Good flowers are picked before they fully open and dried whole, so a bag of loose petals is a poor sign.

`Q` **Kuding is sold as a single famously bitter Chinese infusion. What is actually in the packet?**
  Two different plants share the name: a holly sold as long dark twisted spears, and a privet sold as small flat leaves. They taste and behave differently. The bitterness is not tea's either, so cutting the steep short does not soften it the way it would a green.

`Q` **Monk fruit sweetens an infusion powerfully and adds almost no sugar. What is doing that?**
  Mogrosides, a group of compounds the fruit builds that read as sweet far below the concentration sugar needs, while carrying almost no energy. They hold up to boiling, which is why luo han guo is simmered into soups and cough syrups rather than only steeped.

### Trade

`Q` **Most Kenyan and Ceylon tea is sold through auction rooms in Mombasa and Colombo. What does that do to the tea itself?**
  A buyer bids off a small sample and a grade name, often without tasting widely. So leaf has to be made to hit that grade reliably, rather than to be interesting. It is much of why CTC dominates Kenya, and why a garden's identity survives better sold direct.

`Q` **A tea is sold as bought direct from the farmer. What has usually actually been cut out?**
  Usually the anonymous wholesale layer and the middlemen, not the pooling itself. The contact is often still a village station gathering several growers' leaf. Real single-farm buying exists at the top end, but nothing certifies the claim the way an organic label is certified.

### Uva

`Q` **A July Uva from Sri Lanka smells of menthol and wintergreen. Where does that come from?**
  Stress. From July the kachchan wind comes down off the mountains dry and warm, leaving Uva in a rain shadow, and the leaf answers by raising methyl salicylate, the wintergreen compound. It lasts a few weeks a year. The rest of the estate's crop does not taste like it.

### Water

`·` **Why does the same leaf taste different at home than it did in the shop?**
  Usually the water rather than the tea. Mineral content changes both extraction and aroma perception: hard water mutes delicate aromatics and flattens greens, while very soft water can leave a tea tasting thin. Most specialists target low to moderate mineralisation.

`·` **Two waters have the same hardness and one of them still flattens the tea. Why?**
  Alkalinity: the bicarbonate in the water, measured separately from the calcium and magnesium that make it hard. Bicarbonate neutralises the tea's own acids and lifts the brew pH, so the liquor darkens and the aroma goes flat. Low alkalinity matters more than low hardness.

`Q` **Water boils at about 93C two thousand metres up. What does that do to a tightly rolled oolong brewed there?**
  Boiling point falls with air pressure, so a kettle on Lishan, at 1600m in Taiwan, tops out near 93C and cannot be pushed past it. A hard ball of leaf needs heat to unfurl, so it opens late and the first infusions come out weak. More leaf, or longer pours, is the answer.

### White tea

`·` **Why does white tea keep developing in storage when green tea merely goes stale?**
  White tea is only withered and dried. There is no fixing step, so its enzymes are never fully deactivated and slow transformation continues. Aged Shou Mei is a recognised category. Green tea's enzymes are killed during fixing, so it can only degrade.

`·` **White tea is called unprocessed. What actually happens to it?**
  A long wither, one to three days, then a low drying. No heat is used to stop it and the leaf is never rolled, so a little oxidation creeps in anyway. The names are picking standards: Silver Needle is buds alone, Bai Mu Dan, white peony, a bud with a leaf or two.

`·` **Silver Needle, a white tea of buds alone, looks furred and silver, and the cup fills with tiny floating hairs. What are they?**
  Fine hairs the bud grows to shield itself from sun and insects. They are what make it look silver, and they come loose in hot water. So a faint haze of hairs in the cup is a sign of bud-heavy leaf, not a fault. The Chinese is bai hao, white down.

`Q` **Two Fujian white teas, one from Fuding and one from Zhenghe. What is chiefly making them taste different?**
  White tea is almost entirely its wither, and the two places wither differently. Fuding is coastal and mild, and breaks the long air-drying with short spells of open sun: fresher, downier, sweeter. Zhenghe is inland, higher and colder, and withers under a roof: honey and dried dates.

`Q` **White tea's cheapest grade, Shou Mei, is the one most often laid down for years. Why not the buds?**
  Shou Mei is the late, large-leaf picking, and mature leaf holds far more sugar and polysaccharide than a bud, so there is more in it to change: years take it toward jujube, honey and something medicinal. A bud is prized for what it is now, and time mostly costs it that.

### Wuyi

`Q` **Da Hong Pao, the most famous of the roasted Wuyi rock oolongs, is sold in every shop in northern Fujian. What is almost certainly in the bag?**
  Picking the mother bushes stopped in 2006, so nobody sells their leaf. Most Da Hong Pao is a blended roast of Wuyi cultivars, usually Shui Xian and Rou Gui, built to a house style. Qi Dan is a genuine cutting off the originals; Bei Dou tests as something else.

`Q` **Lapsang Souchong is smoked over pine. When in the making does the smoke go in?**
  It is built in, not added on. At Tongmu, in the Wuyi hills of northern Fujian, the leaf sits in a wooden smokehouse over a pine fire. It takes smoke while it withers, and again while it dries. The campfire version is an export style; the local one is faintly smoky.

`Q` **Two Wuyi rock oolongs from northern Fujian, roasted alike: Rou Gui, named for cassia bark, and Shui Xian, an old large-leaf bush. Which tastes how?**
  Cultivar, showing through one process. Rou Gui is named for cassia bark and pushes a cinnamon-sweet aroma out front. Shui Xian is an old large-leaf cultivar giving a thicker, honeyed, woodier cup. The Wuyi saying: none more aromatic, none more mellow.

`Q` **A Wuyi rock oolong, from the cliffs of northern Fujian, is offered as zhengyan, banyan or zhoucha. What do those name?**
  Three positions, from the cliff outward. The core ravines are zhengyan, true rock. The lower ground around them is banyan, half rock. Along the streams sits zhoucha, sandbank tea, on soil deep and rich enough that the bush grows fast and the cup comes out thinner.

`Q` **Jin Jun Mei sells for more than almost any other Chinese black tea. What is actually in the tin?**
  Buds only, picked before they open, if it is genuine. Made at Tongmu in 2005, the Wuyi village behind pine-smoked Lapsang Souchong, as an unsmoked luxury off the same bushes. The name was never trademarked, so most tins now hold leaf as well as bud.

`Q` **What makes a Wuyi tea a rock oolong, rather than just an oolong that happens to grow at Wuyi?**
  Two things together: the ground and the fire. Yancha means rock tea, off the eroded cliffs and ravines of the Wuyi mountains in northern Fujian, and the style is finished by charcoal roasting repeated over months. Da Hong Pao, Rou Gui and Shui Xian are the names you meet.

### Yellow tea

`·` **Yellow tea is made almost exactly like green tea. What is the extra step?**
  Once the leaf is fixed it is wrapped warm and slightly damp for hours or days. The enzymes are already dead, so this is not oxidation: heat and moisture break chlorophyll down and soften the catechins, taking off the grassy edge. The step is men huang, sealed yellowing.

`·` **Yellow tea is the rarest of the six Chinese classes. What keeps producers off it?**
  The sealed yellowing that makes the class adds days of warm damp handling to a crop that has to be sold fresh, and it can go wrong. The gain is subtle enough that many buyers cannot pick it from a good green. Green tea is quicker, safer and better paid.

### Yunnan

`Q` **Dian Hong, the black tea of Yunnan, is thick and malty where a Fujian black tea is fine and floral. What is behind that?**
  The plant, not the making. Yunnan grows the big-leaf assamica that also becomes puerh, far heavier in polyphenol than the small-leaf bushes of the east coast. Dian Hong is not ancient either: it was set up in 1938, when war cut China off from its eastern black tea districts.

`Q` **Puerh, Dian Hong and China's wild tea forests all come out of Yunnan. What does that province have that the eastern ones do not?**
  The plant. Yunnan is where large-leaf assamica grows wild, in forest rather than hedge, and where seed-grown trees of real age still stand. The eastern provinces work small-leaf sinensis in clipped plantations. One species, a different plant, a different tea.
